slides.title: The questions this chapter answers

items: Which parts does a Bitcoin transaction consist of, what does each part contribute, and what are the values of each part in the real transaction that chapter 2 follows?
Which mathematical tools does a transaction rely on - hashing, key pairs, the elliptic curve, signatures, checksums - and what exactly does each of them guarantee and not guarantee?
How does a payment begin: what does the invoice of the chapter contain, which document defines its format, and what is the status of that document today?
How does a signed transaction reach the miners, who takes part in that journey, and how much of a payment can each kind of participant verify for itself?
How is a transaction recorded: how is a block built, what makes it valid, how is the miner paid, and how are the numbers of the reward, the target and the hash rate obtained?

slides.notes: These are the competency questions the chapter's ontology was written to answer, so they are a fair statement of what a student should be able to answer at the end. Come back to them in the recap. A student who can answer all of them has the chapter; a student who can answer none of them has memorised vocabulary.

slides.title: Transaction
slides.sub: A transaction is the unit of action in Bitcoin: a message telling the network that the owner of certain bitcoins has authorized the transfer of that value to another owner.
slides.notes:
Everything else in Bitcoin exists to carry transactions safely. The network propagates them, miners gather them into blocks and the blockchain records them, so a student who knows what a transaction contains, and how transactions refer to one another, has the vocabulary for the rest of the course. The book adds a point that is easy to miss: bitcoins do not exist physically or as digital data that could be emailed. What exists is a database on every full node that says who controls how many bitcoins, and a transaction is the data that convinces the nodes to update that database (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two cautions apply from the start. A transaction does not move coins from one place to another: it changes who may spend certain outputs, because the book says there are no physical coins or even individual digital coins and that the coins are implied in transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And this chapter simplifies on purpose: it names the signature, the script and the identifier without opening them, so each is given a concept here and a full treatment in a later chapter.

slides.title: Transaction part

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: A transaction part is one of the pieces a transaction is assembled from.

The concepts of this group are taken in the order in which a transaction is read: the double-entry ledger, which supplies the bookkeeping picture that holds the parts together, then the input, the output, the fee…

slides.notes:
Reading a transaction correctly means knowing which part does which job. An input says what is being spent and who allows it, an output says what is created and who may spend it next, and the fee is whatever remains. Confusing these parts leads to the classic misunderstandings, such as believing that a payment is a single amount sent from one address to another.

The parts are met in every block explorer, which retrieves a transaction and shows what it spends and what it creates, and in every wallet that has to assemble them. The chapter's own illustration shows Alice's payment to Bob's store as one transaction whose input is an earlier output and whose two outputs are the payment and the change. The same transaction is printed byte by byte in the book's chapter on transactions, which lets this course check every figure in its description.

Concepts in this section: Double-entry ledger, Input, Output, Transaction fee, Transaction size, Fee rate, Unspent transaction output, Transaction identifier, Script, Serialization, Byte order, Outpoint, Witness.

slides.title: Double-entry ledger

items.head: What it is
items.body: A ledger is a book of record in which each movement of value is written down as an entry, and double-entry bookkeeping is the practice of recording every movement from two sides: what leaves one account and what arrives in another. The chapter uses this picture directly.

items.head: How it works
items.body: In an ordinary ledger the two sides of an entry balance exactly.

slides.notes:
The image gives a student a first mental model for something that has no physical form. Instead of thinking of coins travelling between wallets, one thinks of entries in a shared book, each entry saying which earlier entries it consumes and which new ones it creates. The same image explains why the blockchain is described as the authoritative journal of all transactions: a journal is the chronological book in which such entries are first written down (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The analogy is a teaching device and has limits. A bookkeeper's ledger names accounts and their owners, while a Bitcoin transaction names no person: it refers to earlier outputs and to conditions for spending the new ones. The transaction data also has no field for a running balance per owner. A balance is computed by a wallet, which adds up the unspent outputs it can spend.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Input

items.head: What it is
items.body: An input is the part of a transaction that spends funds. It does not contain coins; it points to an earlier transaction's output, and it carries the proof that the person spending is entitled to do so.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The book's chapter on transactions calls the reference that an input contains an outpoint.

slides.notes:
Inputs are what turn separate transactions into a connected history. Because every input names the output it consumes, anyone can follow a payment backward through the chain of ownership, and anyone can see whether the same output is being spent twice. The proof of ownership in the input, a digital signature that can be independently validated by anyone, is what lets strangers accept a payment without knowing who the payer is (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

An input cannot be partly spent, in the same way that a banknote cannot be torn in two: the whole of the referenced output is consumed, and any surplus must be sent back to the payer as change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word input also invites a misreading. It does not mean money entering an account, but an earlier output being used up. And a figure is a simplification: when a detail matters, such as which output of the earlier transaction is meant, read it from the transaction itself.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Output and Transaction fee

items.head: Output
items.body: An output is the part of a transaction that receives funds. It consists of an amount, counted in satoshis, and a script, the condition that must be satisfied to spend that amount later.
A transaction can have several outputs, and they are numbered from zero in the order in which they appear, which is what the second half of an outpoint refers to.

items.head: Transaction fee
items.body: The transaction fee is a small payment to the miner who includes a transaction in a block. It is never written in the transaction as a separate number.

For Alice's payment the arithmetic is simple. Her input is Tx1's output of 100000 satoshis, the two outputs total 95000 satoshis, and so 100000 - sum([75000, 20000]) evaluates to 5000: the fee is 5000 satoshis.

slides.notes:
Outputs are where ownership is created. The chapter explains that an output is created with a script saying, in effect, that it is paid to whoever can present a signature from the key corresponding to Bob's public address. Because only Bob's wallet holds that key, only Bob can later spend the output. The book calls this encumbering the output with a demand for a signature from Bob (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Outputs are all-or-nothing in the same way as inputs: a later transaction takes a whole output or leaves it alone. An output also never expires. It stays unspent, and is counted in every full node's database, until a valid transaction spends it, which is why the book warns that outputs of very small value can become uneconomical to spend and are a burden on the nodes that must keep track of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

---

The fee is how a user asks the network to process a payment in a timely fashion. The chapter on fees explains that it is not a fee in the usual sense: it is not an amount set by the protocol or by any miner, but much more like a bid in an auction for the limited space in a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is one of two payments that reward a miner, the other being the newly created bitcoins of the block reward. Nakamoto's paper already described it: if the output value of a transaction is less than its input value, the difference is a fee added to the incentive of the block containing the transaction (Nakamoto, 2008).

Because the fee is implied, a wallet that mistakes the amounts can send an enormous fee without any warning from the format, since there is no field to check. Wallets should therefore make it hard to pay an excessive fee by accident, while still allowing it on purpose, as the chapter on fees advises (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Fees also do not depend on the value being sent, but on how much space the transaction takes, which the concepts of size and fee rate explain.

slides.title: Transaction size and Fee rate

items.head: Transaction size
items.body: The size of a transaction is the room that it takes up in a block. Because every block can hold only a limited amount of transaction data, software needs a measure for it.
The weight of a transaction is the sum of the weights of its fields, each field's serialized size in bytes being multiplied by a factor (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: Fee rate
items.body: The fee rate is the fee a transaction pays for each unit of the space it takes in a block.
The calculation is a plain division. Alice's payment paid 5000 satoshis and takes up 143 virtual bytes, so its fee rate is 5000 / 143, which rounds to 34.97 satoshis per virtual byte.

slides.notes:
Size is what makes block space a scarce good. A block is limited to 4 million units of weight, so the number of transactions that fit depends on how large each one is, not on how much value it moves (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A payment of a million bitcoins and one of a single satoshi may occupy the same room, and a miner who has to choose between them looks at the fee that each pays for that room, which is the idea behind the fee rate.

The three numbers answer different questions. The size in bytes is the length of the serialized data, the weight is what the block limit counts, and the virtual byte is the weight expressed in a familiar unit. Mixing them up is a common reason for fee figures that do not match between two tools. The factors themselves belong to a later chapter on transactions, and a student should treat the number 4 as a fixed part of today's rules, not a law of nature.

---

Block space is scarce, and the fee rate is the price at which it is sold. A transaction pays a single fee however large it is, but a larger transaction leaves room for fewer others in the block, so a miner who wants the most revenue from a block fills it with the transactions that pay the highest fee per unit of space. The chapter says accordingly that transactions are added to a new block prioritized by the highest fee rate first (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The units are a source of expensive mistakes. The book warns that a fee rate copied from a field with one denominator into a field with another can lead to paying a thousand times too much, and that switching the numerator could mean a hundred million times too much (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fee rate is also a market price, not a rule of the protocol, so what counts as a good rate changes with demand for block space; the figure of 34.97 describes one payment, not a recommendation.

slides.title: Unspent transaction output

items.head: What it is
items.body: An unspent transaction output, abbreviated UTXO, is a transaction output that has not yet been used as an input by any later transaction. The glossary defines it as an unspent transaction output that can be spent as an input in a new transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet's bitcoins are, in this sense, nothing other than the unspent outputs it can unlock.

rows: [o for o, spent in {'Tx1:0': True, 'Tx2:0': False, 'Tx2:1': False}.items() if not spent]

items.head: How it works
items.body: Mark each output with a flag that says whether it has been spent.

slides.notes:
The idea explains how Bitcoin keeps track of ownership without accounts. A full node holds a copy of every confirmed transaction's unspent outputs, and a valid new transaction may spend only outputs that are in that set. Each time a new block arrives, the outputs that its transactions spend are removed from the database and the outputs they create are added, so the set of unspent outputs is the current state of the whole system, and a double-spend is simply an attempt to use an output that is already gone (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two misreadings are common. An unspent output is not an account balance, and a wallet's total is the sum of many separate outputs, each of which is spent whole. And an unspent output is still tied to a condition: it counts as spendable only for the party that can satisfy its script. Wallets therefore track UTXOs for their own keys and ignore the rest.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Transaction identifier

items.head: What it is
items.body: The transaction identifier, or txid, is the 32-byte name of a transaction. It is derived from the transaction's own data by a hash function, so it is not assigned by anyone, and two different transactions cannot sensibly share one. In the chapter the txid is what an input uses to refer to the transaction in which funds were received (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Bitcoin Core computes the identifier by hashing the serialized transaction without its proof data (Bitcoin Core, 2026); hashing means applying the double SHA-256 construction that the concept of the hash function shows, and the result is shown with its bytes reversed. Doing exactly that to the 194 bytes of Alice's real transaction reproduces the printed identifier.

slides.notes:
Names make references possible. Because a txid summarizes the transaction it identifies, a reference to it cannot be redirected to different content, and anyone holding the transaction can recompute the name and confirm it. This is also what makes a chain of transactions auditable: every link is a txid plus a position, and both can be checked independently by any node.

A txid belongs to the transaction as it was built, and it is not proof that the transaction has been confirmed: a payment can have a txid and still wait in the mempool. The byte-order difference is a frequent source of confusion for programmers: pasting the stored form into a block explorer, or the displayed form into a program that expects the stored one, finds nothing, because the hash is the same and only its reading differs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Script

items.head: What it is
items.body: A script is a small program written in Bitcoin's own scripting language, called Script.

rows: [s.append(s.pop() + s.pop()) if t == 'OP_ADD' else s.append(s.pop() == s.pop()) if t == 'OP_EQUAL' else s.append(int(t)) for t in '2 3 OP_ADD 5 OP_EQUAL'.split()] and s

items.head: How it works
items.body: Script is a stack-based language: it reads items from left to right, pushes numbers onto a stack, and operators remove items from the stack, act on them and may push a result back. The book's first example is the script 2 3 OP_ADD 5 OP_EQUAL.

slides.notes:
Scripts are what make spending conditions flexible without making the rules of the network complicated. The first version of Bitcoin did not simply attach a public key to an output; it let payments go to an output script and let the spender answer with an input script, so that conditions such as needing two signatures out of two keys could be expressed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's chapter on keys states the idea in one sentence: bitcoins are received to an output script that acts like a public key, and spending is authorized by an input script that acts like a signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Script is deliberately limited. It has no loops and only conditional flow control, so it is not Turing complete, which guarantees predictable execution times; and it is stateless, so a script behaves the same way on every system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's arithmetic example is also a warning: an output with the script 3 OP_ADD 5 OP_EQUAL can be spent by anyone who knows that the number 2 satisfies it, because a script grants authority to whoever can satisfy it, not to a named person (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Serialization

items.head: What it is
items.body: Serialization is the writing of a structured object as a flat sequence of bytes, in an order and a format on which sender and receiver agree, so that the receiver can rebuild the same structure. A transaction in a wallet is a structure of inputs, outputs and amounts; a transaction on the network is a string of bytes.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The format is a sequence of fixed and variable fields.

slides.notes:
Everything exact in this chapter depends on the serialized form. The identifier of a transaction is a hash of its bytes, so the bytes must be defined to the last detail; the size that a fee pays for is the length of those bytes; and the signature commits to them. If two programs serialized the same transaction differently they would compute different identifiers and the network would not work. This is why the description of the format belongs to the consensus-critical part of Bitcoin and not to a matter of taste.

A serialized transaction is not readable by eye, and it is not encrypted either: it is simply a precise encoding, and anyone with the format can decode it. Two cautions follow. First, the identifier is computed from the serialization without the witness data, so the same payment has two byte-lengths and two hashes, which the concepts of the identifier and of the size explain. Second, the hexadecimal string is a printing of the bytes, not the bytes themselves, so a program must decode the text before hashing it.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Byte order

items.head: What it is
items.body: Byte order, also called endianness, is the direction in which the individual bytes of a multi-byte value are written down. Writing the most significant byte first is called big-endian and is what people do when they write ordinary numbers; writing the least significant byte first is called little-endian and is what most processors do internally.

items.head: How it works
items.body: Reversing a sequence of bytes converts between the two readings.

slides.notes:
Bitcoin uses both orders, and the mismatch is a standing source of confusion that the book itself warns about: hash digests are displayed to users in one byte order but are used internally in a different byte order (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student who does not know this will conclude that the identifier stored inside Alice's input is a different transaction from the one her wallet shows, and a programmer who does not know it will search a block explorer for a hash that exists and find nothing.

Three practical rules follow. Reverse bytes, never characters. Reverse only values that the convention requires, which in this chapter means transaction and block hashes, not the witness or the output scripts. And when a tool reports something that does not match, try the other order before concluding that the data is wrong, because the book's note about the two byte orders applies to almost every hash a reader will paste from one program into another (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Outpoint

items.head: What it is
items.body: An outpoint is the exact name of one transaction output: the identifier of the transaction that created it together with the position of that output within the transaction.

items.head: How it works
items.body: An outpoint is formed by putting the two parts together, as the small example does by joining an abbreviated identifier and the index with a colon.

slides.notes:
The outpoint is the link that makes the whole structure of Bitcoin work. Because an input names one and only one earlier output, a node can look it up, learn the amount and the spending condition, and check whether it is still unspent; and because the identifier is a hash, the reference cannot be redirected to other content. The set of unspent outputs that a full node keeps is in effect a table indexed by outpoints, so the double-spend check is a lookup of one outpoint.

Two warnings. The index counts from zero, so the first output of a transaction is output 0 and the familiar off-by-one error here means spending the wrong output or none at all. And an outpoint is not an address and not an owner: it identifies a position in the ledger, and who may spend it is decided by the script in the output it names, which is why a chain of outpoints can be followed without learning anybody's identity.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Witness

items.head: What it is
items.body: The witness of an input is the data that proves the input may be spent.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The figures can be read out of the transaction.

slides.notes:
The separation matters for two reasons that this chapter has already met. The first is the identifier: because the witness is left out of the data that is hashed, the identifier of a transaction no longer changes when the proof changes, which removes a family of problems the book lists as circular dependence and third-party and second-party malleability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is size: the witness bytes are counted once in the weight while the rest are counted four times, which is why spending an output is cheaper than it would otherwise be and why the three size figures of a transaction differ.

Do not read the separation as hiding: the witness is public, it is sent to every node and it is committed to by the block, so nothing about it is secret. Note also that the word has two uses that the book keeps apart, the witness as the abstract name for authorizing data and the witness structure as the field that carries it, and that the course's later chapters on authorization open both. Finally, a transaction with no witness at all is serialized in the older format, so a program that assumes the two marker bytes are always present will misread such a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Cryptographic foundations

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: A transaction asks every computer on the network to believe something without trusting anyone: that the person spending certain bitcoins is entitled to spend them. Mathematics alone makes that possible, and this group collects the mathematical tools on which the rest of the chapter silently relies.
The concepts of the group are taken in the order in which a learner needs them. The hash function comes first because the others use it.

slides.notes:
Almost every later concept of the chapter is built from these tools. A transaction identifier is a hash, a block is identified by a hash, mining is a search for a hash with a special property, and an input is accepted only when it carries a signature that was made with the right private key. A reader who does not know what a hash or a signature guarantees cannot judge what the network can and cannot promise. The book's own chapter on keys says it will examine public keys, private keys, signatures and hash functions and then use all of them together to describe addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two warnings are in order. First, these tools are quite different in what they promise: a hash function provides no secrecy, a signature provides no secrecy either, and neither is the same thing as encryption. Second, a clever tool is only as safe as its use. The book warns that anything less than completely random when a private key is chosen can significantly reduce the security of the key and of the bitcoins it controls (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Read each concept below with the question what exactly does this guarantee, and what does it leave open?

Concepts in this section: Hash function, Key pair, Public-key cryptography, Elliptic curve, Digital signature, Checksum, Bit and byte, Hexadecimal notation, Entropy, Nonce, Encryption.

slides.title: Hash function
slides.sub: a fixed-size fingerprint of any data

items.head: What it is
items.body: A hash function is a procedure that takes data of any length, however long or short, scrambles it thoroughly and outputs a value of fixed length, which is called the hash or the digest of the data. The book describes it as a function that takes a potentially large amount of data, scrambles it, and outputs a fixed amount of data, and it points out two properties.

items.head: How it works
items.body: You can try it directly.

slides.notes:
Because of these two properties a digest works as a commitment: it is a promise that, in practice, only one input produces it. This lets Bitcoin refer to large objects by a short name that nobody can redirect to something else. A hash is also the raw material of mining, since the network's lottery is a search for an input whose hash falls below a threshold, and nobody can find such an input except by trying one after another (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Without hash functions Bitcoin would need a central party to say what a transaction or a block is.

A hash function is not encryption. It has no key and no way back, so you cannot recover the input from the digest, but if the possible inputs are few, anyone can simply hash all of them and compare. A digest also says nothing about who made the data: anyone can compute it. And the guarantee that two different inputs will not give the same digest is a statement about the effort needed to find such a pair, not an absolute impossibility, because a function with a fixed-length output must map many inputs to the same output; the book calls such a pair a collision and says finding one is computationally infeasible (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Key pair
slides.sub: a secret number and the public value made from it

items.head: What it is
items.body: A key pair consists of two numbers that belong together: a private key and a public key. In Bitcoin the private key is a number, usually derived from a number picked at random, and the public key is calculated from it by a mathematical operation that is easy in one direction and impractical in the other.

The private key can be any number from 0 up to n minus 1, where n is a constant slightly smaller than 2 to the power 256, defined as the order of the elliptic curve that Bitcoin uses; to create one, software picks a random 256-bit number and checks that it is below n (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.notes:
The pair separates two abilities that ordinary passwords combine. Anyone may be told the public key, and with it can receive funds or check a signature, but only the holder of the private key can produce a valid signature. The book says that control over the private key is the root of user control over all funds associated with the corresponding public key, and that revealing the private key to third parties is equivalent to giving them control over the bitcoins it secures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same text adds that a lost private key cannot be recovered, and the funds it secured are lost forever.

The private key is a number, not a file or a word, and its secrecy depends entirely on how it was chosen. The book advises against writing one's own random number generator and recommends a cryptographically secure generator seeded with enough entropy, because a process that is less than completely random can significantly reduce the security of the key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The public key cannot be turned back into the private key by the known mathematics, but this is a statement about today's computers and algorithms, not a proof that it can never be done.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Public-key cryptography

items.head: What it is
items.body: Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is a branch of cryptography in which each participant has two related keys instead of one shared secret. One key can be made public and the other must stay private.

rows: [k for k in range(1, 17) if pow(3, k, 17) == 11]

items.head: How it works
items.body: A tiny example shows the idea of a one-way function.

slides.notes:
Before this invention, two parties who wanted to protect a message needed to share a secret in advance, which does not scale to a network of strangers. Public-key cryptography removes that need. The book explains that in Bitcoin it is not used to encrypt transactions, because transactions are public. Its useful property is the ability to generate digital signatures: a private key can be applied to a transaction to produce a signature that only someone who knows the private key could have made, yet anyone with the public key and the transaction can verify it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The security is conditional. It depends on the assumption that no efficient method of reversing the function is known, and on the keys having been chosen at random; the book says that the private key must stay secret at all times and be protected from accidental loss (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word public must not be misread: the public key may be shared, but the private key must never be. Note, too, that signing is not encrypting, so a Bitcoin transaction is readable by everyone, and its privacy rests on other things, such as the fact that addresses name no person.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Elliptic curve
slides.sub: the curve y squared equals x cubed plus 7

items.head: What it is
items.body: An elliptic curve is the set of points whose two coordinates satisfy a certain cubic equation. Bitcoin uses one particular curve, defined in a standard called secp256k1, whose equation is the very simple y squared equals x cubed plus 7.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The curve secp256k1 is fixed by the constants p, the generator point G and the order n.

slides.notes:
Points on an elliptic curve can be added to each other by a geometric rule, and adding a point to itself repeatedly gives multiplication of a point by a whole number. This multiplication is easy to carry out but, when the numbers are large, practically impossible to undo: given the result, finding the number is the discrete logarithm problem. The book calls this a trap door function and says it is the basis for unforgeable and secure digital signatures that prove control over bitcoin funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin's choice of this particular curve and its constants is part of the protocol, so every implementation must use exactly the same ones.

The picture of a smooth curve in textbooks is misleading for Bitcoin. With a finite field the curve is a cloud of points in a very large grid, and the geometric rule of tangent lines and reflections is only an analogy for the algebra that is actually computed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Writing your own implementation of the mathematics is also dangerous: simple code like that in the examples of this course is not protected against timing attacks, and real wallets use carefully reviewed libraries.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Digital signature
slides.sub: a proof made with the private key

items.head: What it is
items.body: A digital signature is a number, or a pair of numbers, calculated from a message and a private key, which anyone can check against the corresponding public key.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The mechanism can be run with the textbook ECDSA formulas on the curve of the previous concept. Using the book's example private key, the program signs the message pay Bob 75000 and obtains two numbers r and s; checking them against the public key returns True.

slides.notes:
The chapter says that a transaction contains proof of ownership for each amount being spent, in the form of a digital signature from the owner that can be independently validated by anyone (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The later chapter on signatures lists three purposes: the signature proves that the controller of the private key has authorized the spending, the proof cannot be denied afterwards, and the authorized transaction cannot be changed by unauthenticated third parties (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Together these replace the bank's signature card and the clerk's judgement with a calculation that thousands of independent nodes can repeat.

A signature is tied to what was signed. Bitcoin lets a signer choose, with a flag called SIGHASH, which part of the transaction the signature commits to, so a signature is not simply a stamp on the whole document (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The signature also does not identify a person: it shows only that someone controlling the private key authorized this transaction. Finally, forging a signature without the private key is believed infeasible, not proven impossible, and a stolen private key lets a thief sign validly, with no way for the network to tell.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Checksum
slides.sub: a few bytes of hash that catch typing errors

items.head: What it is
items.body: A checksum is a short piece of data calculated from a longer piece and attached to it, so that a recipient can recompute it and see whether the longer piece was damaged on the way.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The older method is easy to run. The checksum of the data is the first four bytes of the double-SHA256 hash of the data.

slides.notes:
Addresses are typed, spoken, copied and photographed by people, and a single wrong character could send funds to an address that nobody controls. A checksum turns that silent loss into an immediate error message. The book says that it prevents a mistyped Bitcoin address from being accepted by the wallet software as a valid destination, an error that would otherwise result in loss of funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bech32 goes further: in an address of the expected length it is guaranteed to detect any error affecting four characters or fewer, and for an address typed with a few errors it can tell the user where the errors are (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A checksum detects accidents, not attacks. An adversary who changes the data can simply compute a new matching checksum, so a checksum protects against a mistyped character but not against a malicious substitution, for which one needs a signature. The guarantee of bech32 also holds only if the length is unchanged: the book reports that in the original bech32 design it was easy to add or remove letters q before a final p without invalidating the checksum, a weakness that the later bech32m variant was made to remove (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Bit and byte

items.head: What it is
items.body: A bit is the smallest unit of digital information: a single binary digit that is either 0 or 1. A byte is a group of eight bits, and it is the unit in which computers normally measure the length of data. The two units describe the same thing at different granularities, so one length can always be converted into the other by multiplying or dividing by eight.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The conversion is a multiplication by eight.

slides.notes:
The chapter cannot be read without them. The book says that the output of SHA256 is always 256 bits long whatever the size of the input, that an input refers to an earlier transaction by a 32-byte identifier, and that output indexes are 4-byte unsigned integers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). These are the same kind of statement, and a reader who cannot move between the two units will think that a 256-bit hash and a 32-byte hash are different objects. Precise sizes also matter for a different reason: the room a transaction takes in a block is counted in bytes, and that is what its fee buys.

Watch the capital letter and the prefix. A lowercase b usually means bit and a capital B means byte, so 1 MB and 1 Mb differ by a factor of eight. Prefixes are also ambiguous: a kilobyte may mean 1,000 or 1,024 bytes depending on the author, which is one reason the book quotes the block limit as a weight of 4,000,000 rather than in megabytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And a byte is not a character: text becomes bytes only after an encoding is chosen, which is why the standard for payment requests has to say that each octet of the UTF-8 sequence is percent-encoded (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Hexadecimal notation and Entropy

items.head: Hexadecimal notation
items.body: Hexadecimal notation writes numbers in base sixteen, using the ten digits 0 to 9 and then the letters a to f for the values ten to fifteen.

Converting is a matter of weighted digits. The two-digit value ff stands for fifteen sixteens plus fifteen, that is 255, the largest value a byte can hold; the four-byte value 1d00ffff read as one number is 486,604,799.

items.head: Entropy
items.body: Entropy, in the sense used in cryptography, is a measure of how unpredictable a value is to someone who does not know it.
Counting entropy is counting possibilities.

slides.notes:
Almost every value this chapter quotes is written in hexadecimal: the transaction identifier, the block hash, the private key, the address's underlying program, the compact form of the mining target. Without the notation these would have to be printed as enormous decimal numbers in which no part corresponds to a field. The notation is also what lets a reader check a length at a glance, since the book's remark that 64 hexadecimal characters display 32 bytes is just the statement that two digits make a byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two traps are worth naming. The first is that hexadecimal is only a notation: the identifier of a transaction is 32 bytes of data, not 64 characters of text, and a program that hashes the printed form instead of the bytes gets a completely different answer. The second is the order in which the bytes are written down, which Bitcoin does differently in different places; the concept of byte order explains that trap in detail.

---

Every guarantee in this chapter that rests on a secret rests on entropy. A private key is only safe because an attacker would have to search an unimaginably large space, and that space is large only if the key was really chosen at random. The book makes the point sharply: it advises the reader not to write their own code to create a random number, to use a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator seeded with sufficient entropy, and it warns that any process that is less than completely random can significantly reduce the security of the private key and of the bitcoins it controls (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Entropy cannot be judged by looking at a value. A key full of apparently random digits may have been produced by a predictable generator, and the result will look exactly as unguessable as a real one. Nor does more entropy help anywhere else: the chapter's hashes, identifiers and addresses are public values, and adding randomness to them changes nothing. Entropy matters only for the values that must stay secret, which in this chapter means the private key behind the signature.

slides.title: Nonce
slides.sub: a number used once to vary a result

items.head: What it is
items.body: A nonce is a value that is varied in order to change the output of a cryptographic function without changing the data that is really being protected. The word is a contraction of number used once.

rows: next(n for n in range(1000) if hashlib.sha256(('Hello, world! %d\n' % n).encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0'))

items.head: How it works
items.body: The book's own miniature example can be run.

slides.notes:
A nonce is what turns a fixed, deterministic function into something that can be searched. A hash function always gives the same output for the same input, so a miner who wants a different output must change the input, and the nonce is the field reserved for that purpose. In signing, the nonce serves the opposite purpose: it makes two signatures over the same message different, which is necessary for the mathematics of the signature scheme to stay secure. The book describes the signing step as first generating a private nonce, and warns that the extra complexity of handling it has in some cases resulted in software accidentally leaking private keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The two nonces must never be confused, because their rules are opposite. The mining nonce is public and may be anything; the signing nonce must be secret and must never be reused, since reusing one with the same key allows the private key to be recovered. A nonce is also not a password or a key: in mining it is simply the part of the input that the searcher is allowed to change, and in signing it is a one-time random value that is thrown away as soon as the signature exists.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Encryption
slides.sub: making data unreadable without a key

items.head: What it is
items.body: Encryption is the transformation of data into a form that cannot be read without a key, together with the matching transformation that turns it back. Its purpose is secrecy.

rows: (bytes(c ^ k for c in m).hex(), bytes(c ^ k for c in bytes(c ^ k for c in m)).decode())

items.head: How it works
items.body: The simplest possible illustration is a reversible operation with a key.

slides.notes:
The distinction decides what is private on a blockchain. The book states plainly that public-key cryptography in Bitcoin is not used to encrypt, that is, to make secret, the transactions, and that its useful property is instead the ability to generate digital signatures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every transaction in this chapter, including Alice's, is therefore readable by anyone: the amounts, the conditions on the outputs and the signature itself are public. What a reader cannot do is forge a signature, and that is a guarantee about authorship, not about secrecy.

Do not expect encryption to give privacy on the blockchain, and do not expect signatures to give secrecy. The book's chapter on keys lists the private key's requirement as remaining secret at all times, which is a matter of storage and not of encrypting transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Note also that encrypting a payment would defeat the system's purpose: nodes must read a transaction in order to verify it, which is why the data is public and the privacy of a user rests on other things, such as the fact that an address names no person.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Linkage

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: A single transaction is only the beginning of the story, because bitcoins are never created in a vacuum: each is spent from something that existed before and gives rise to something that will exist afterwards. This group deals with the links between transactions. It explains the chain that results when each transaction spends the outputs of an earlier one, the change that a spender receives back because an output cannot be partly spent, and the choice that a wallet makes among the outputs it could spend, which is called coin selection.
The group is taken in the order of the story. The transaction chain explains what a link is and how Alice's payment is connected to the payment she received from Joe.

slides.notes:
The links are what turn individual transactions into a history, and the history is what lets any node decide whether a payment is genuine. If Alice's payment spends an output created by Joe's transaction, and that output has not been spent before, the payment is valid in this respect; if it has been spent, the payment is a double spend. The three concepts of the group show how the requirement is met in practice, and also how wallet design decisions leave traces that others can read.

Links are public, and public links can be followed by anybody. A chain of transactions is a record of where each output came from, so the choices that a wallet makes in building the links affect the privacy of its owner. Keep this in mind while reading the concepts: the same facts that make Bitcoin auditable also make it traceable.

Concepts in this section: Transaction chain, Making change, Coin selection.

slides.title: Transaction chain and Making change

items.head: Transaction chain
items.body: A transaction chain is the sequence of transactions that arises when each transaction spends outputs created by an earlier one.
The numbers in the book's illustration make the chain concrete. Tx1 sent 100,000 satoshis to an output locked by Alice's key.

items.head: Making change
items.body: Making change is the practice of adding to a transaction an output that returns the surplus to the person who is paying.
The wallet's arithmetic is a subtraction. With an input worth 100000 satoshis, a payment of 75000 and a fee of 5000, the change is 100000 - 75000 - 5000, which is 20000.

slides.notes:
The chain is the answer to the question of where bitcoins come from and where they have gone. Because each input names the output it consumes, anyone can follow a payment back through the chain of ownership, and the owner of an output can be changed only by a transaction that spends it. When Bob spends the output he received, he extends the chain; the chapter's last illustration shows Alice's transaction as part of a chain from Joe to Gopesh (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same structure underlies the idea of provenance, which the final concepts of this chapter take up.

The figure is a simplification, and the real transaction differs from it in a detail. In the figure Alice's input is labelled Tx1:0, which is the output of 100,000 satoshis, the first of the two outputs drawn for Tx1; but in the bytes of the real transaction the output index stored in the input is 1. The order of Tx2's outputs, by contrast, agrees with the figure: the change of 20,000 satoshis is at position 0 and Bob's 75,000 satoshis at position 1, which is why Tx3 spends Tx2:1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Remember also that a chain of transactions links outputs, not people: it does not say who the owners are, only which outputs were spent to create which others.

---

Without change, every payment would have to match an available output exactly, or the surplus would be given to the miner as an enormous fee. The change output lets a wallet spend any output, whatever its size, and keep the remainder. It also explains why most payments have the same shape: one input and two outputs, one for the receiver and one for the sender (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the sender, the change output is simply a new output that can be spent in a later transaction.

The book hopes that payment and change look identical on the blockchain, since the change address is often a new address of the sender's wallet, for privacy reasons, and a third party could not then tell which output is the change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's real transaction does not fully achieve that ideal: its two output scripts have different lengths, 34 and 22 bytes, so an observer can tell them apart. And the change is not extra money: it is an ordinary output that nobody can use unless the wallet keeps the key, so a wallet that loses the change key loses the change.

slides.title: Coin selection

items.head: What it is
items.body: Coin selection is the process by which a wallet decides which of its unspent outputs to use as inputs in a payment. Different wallets use different strategies.

rows: next((vals[:i + 1], sum(vals[:i + 1]) - need) for i in range(len(vals)) if sum(vals[:i + 1]) >= need)

items.head: How it works
items.body: A simple strategy can be programmed in a few lines.

slides.notes:
The choice has consequences that last. The book compares it with handling cash: if you always use the largest bill in your pocket you end up with a pocket full of loose change, and if you only use the loose change you will often be left with only big bills. People subconsciously find a balance between these extremes, and Bitcoin wallet developers strive to program this balance (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet that always picks small outputs builds large transactions that cost more in fees; one that always picks large outputs creates many small outputs that may later be too small to be worth spending.

The selection is visible to the outside world. Spending several outputs in one transaction shows that one party probably controls all of them, which weakens privacy. And every input costs space and therefore fee, so the cheapest set now is not always the best for later. Treat coin selection as a design decision with several competing aims, and remember that the book presents it as a balance, not as a single correct method.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Form

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Transactions come in a few typical shapes, which this group calls forms. A form is described by how many inputs and outputs a transaction has and by what it is used for. The chapter names three: the simple payment, with one input and two outputs; the consolidation, which spends several inputs into a single output; and payment batching, which pays several recipients with a single transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The group is taken from the commonest to the least common.

slides.notes:
Recognizing the forms helps a reader to interpret what a block explorer displays and to guess what the sender intended. A transaction with many inputs and one output is probably a tidy-up of small amounts, one with many outputs is probably a business paying many people, and one with one input and two outputs is probably an ordinary payment with change. The forms also show that nothing in the format limits a transaction to one payer and one payee.

A form is a description of a typical shape and not a rule of the protocol, which sees only a list of inputs and a list of outputs and checks the same conditions whatever the shape. The names used here are the conventions of the course and of the book, so another text may count the forms differently. A transaction can also combine the features, for example by consolidating many inputs while paying two recipients and returning change, in which case no single name fits. Finally, a form says nothing about who built the transaction or why: the shape is a hint about intention, never evidence of it, and reading too much into it is the mistake that the privacy remarks of this branch warn against.

Concepts in this section: Simple payment, Consolidation, Payment batching.

slides.title: Simple payment and Consolidation

items.head: Simple payment
items.body: A simple payment is the most common form of transaction.

Counting is all that is needed. If the number of inputs is one and the number of outputs is two, and the amounts are 100000 for the input, 75000 and 20000 for the outputs, then the fee is the 5000 that remains.

items.head: Consolidation
items.body: A consolidation transaction spends several inputs into a single output. The book offers a picture from everyday money: it is the real-world equivalent of exchanging a pile of coins and currency notes for a single larger note (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The arithmetic is unchanged: the single output is the sum of the inputs minus the fee.

slides.notes:
The form is common because it is the natural result of how outputs behave. A person usually owns an output that is larger than the item to be bought, an output cannot be partly spent, and so the wallet writes one output for the seller and one back for the buyer. Understanding it explains why Alice's balance after paying Bob is not simply her earlier balance minus 75,000 satoshis in a single step: the old output disappears and a new, smaller one takes its place.

A simple payment is a description, not a promise. Some payments have a single input and a single output, the changeless transactions, and some have a second output that is not change, for instance a donation. The two-output pattern also invites a privacy question: when the outputs have different amounts, an observer may guess that the larger one is the change, or the smaller; the guess is only a guess.

---

Many small outputs are inconvenient. Each needs a separate input when it is spent, and every input adds to the size and therefore to the fee of a later transaction. A wallet or business that has received many small payments can combine them in one transaction, at a time when fees are low, and later pay with a single large output. Because the chapter on coin selection explains that wallets balance small and large outputs, the consolidation can be seen as the inverse of an ordinary payment.

Consolidation has costs that the picture of a single note hides. All the inputs are spent together, and so a watcher can conclude that they probably belong to the same owner, which is a loss of privacy. It must also be paid for now: spending many inputs makes a large transaction, and a large transaction pays a larger total fee than a small one at the same fee rate.

slides.title: Payment batching

items.head: What it is
items.body: Payment batching is the form in which one transaction pays to multiple outputs representing multiple recipients.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The arithmetic is again the same: the inputs equal the outputs plus the fee.

slides.notes:
A business that pays many people would otherwise create a separate transaction for each, and every one of those transactions would carry its own overhead. A batch gathers the payments in one transaction. It is the counterpart of the consolidation: instead of many inputs flowing into one output, one flow of funds is spread to many outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A batch also makes the payer's own accounting simpler, as a single transaction records the whole payroll.

The recipients of a batch can see the other outputs and their amounts, because the transaction is public, so a payroll batch discloses the full list of salaries paid in one transaction to anyone who looks. A batch also depends on a single set of inputs and a single signature step, and a mistake in building it affects every recipient at once.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Unit

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: A unit is a standard quantity in which value is counted, and a currency usually has several of them: one for everyday prices, smaller ones for small change, and sometimes a very small one in which the accounts are actually kept.
The group has a single concept, the satoshi, because every other unit is a plain multiple of it.

slides.notes:
A reader who does not know the units cannot read a transaction or a fee, because the same payment is described by three different numbers depending on the unit chosen. The prices in Bob's store are quoted in dollars and in bitcoin, while the figures in the diagram of the transaction chain are satoshis, because that is what the protocol itself uses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A mistake of the unit is therefore not a small error but a factor of one hundred million, and the chapter on fees warns that confusing the denominator or the numerator of a fee rate can mean overpaying by a thousand or by a hundred million times (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Stating the unit beside every figure is the cheapest possible protection against that class of mistake.

Do not mix units in a calculation, and do not trust a number that arrives without one. Many defects and many costly payments have come from treating a figure in one unit as a figure in another, which is why this course states the unit next to every number it writes down. Two further cautions belong here. The names of the fractions are conventions and not protocol rules, so a wallet may offer units that another wallet has never heard of; and converting a decimal amount in bitcoin into satoshis with ordinary floating-point arithmetic can introduce a small error, which is one reason the protocol counts in whole satoshis in the first place.

Concepts in this section: Satoshi.

slides.title: Satoshi

items.head: What it is
items.body: The satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin that can be recorded in a transaction: one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin, or 0.00000001. The book says the Bitcoin network can transact in fractional values, from the millibitcoin, one thousandth of a bitcoin, down to 1/100,000,000th of a bitcoin, which is known as a satoshi (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: How it works
items.body: The conversions are plain division and multiplication.

slides.notes:
The name has a short history. When Bitcoin was first created, the smallest unit had no name and some developers called it the base unit; later many users began calling it a satoshi in honor of Bitcoin's creator, who published the whitepaper under the name Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The practical importance is that integer arithmetic is exact: the protocol counts whole satoshis and never needs fractions, so there are no rounding errors in the totals of a transaction.

The book states a convention that students often overlook: it uses the same pluralization rules as for dollars, so the text speaks of 10 bitcoins and 0.001 bitcoins, and of millibitcoins and satoshis in the same way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Another caution concerns display: wallets may show amounts in bitcoin or in satoshis, and a user who reads 100000 where 0.001 was expected has made a mistake of a factor of one hundred million in the other direction.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Payment request

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: A payment request is the message through which a seller tells a buyer what to pay, to whom and why. In the chapter the request is created automatically by Bob's e-commerce system as a QR code that holds an invoice, and Alice's wallet reads it so that she never has to type an address or an amount. This group explains the pieces: the address-bearing web link called a URI, the QR code that carries it, the improvement proposal that defines its format, and the invoice itself (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The group begins with the URI, the general kind of web address that the request uses. The QR code is then described as the carrier.

slides.notes:
Typing a long address by hand is slow and error-prone, and an address typed wrongly can lose the payment. A payment request puts the address, the amount and a description into one object that a wallet can read in one step. The book notes that, unlike a QR code that simply contains a destination address, the invoice is a QR-encoded URI that contains a destination address, a payment amount and a description, so that the wallet application can prefill the information and show a human-readable description to the user (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The request itself is not a transaction. Nothing is sent to the network when a code is displayed or scanned, and the buyer can decline. The format is also only a convenience: a wallet must still ask the user to approve the payment, and the standard itself says that clients must not act on such a URI without getting the user's authorization (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

Concepts in this section: Uniform resource identifier, QR code, Bitcoin improvement proposal, BIP21 URI, Bitcoin address, Exchange rate.

slides.title: Uniform resource identifier
slides.sub: a scheme, a path and a query

items.head: What it is
items.body: A uniform resource identifier, URI, is a string of characters that names or locates something according to a general format.

items.head: How it works
items.body: Python's standard library splits a URI into its parts.

slides.notes:
A common format lets different programs cooperate without knowing about each other. A web page or a QR code can carry a link, the operating system can recognize the scheme, and the wallet that registered itself for it can open it. The standard says the purpose of the scheme is to enable users to easily make payments by simply clicking links on webpages or scanning QR codes, and recommends that graphical bitcoin clients register themselves as the handler for the bitcoin: scheme (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

A URI is text, and text can be forged. A link on a web page can show one thing and contain another, and a malicious page can offer an address that is not the seller's. That is the reason for the rule that a wallet may not act on a URI without the user's authorization, and why the user should compare the address and amount shown by the wallet with what was expected (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: QR code
slides.sub: a square of black and white dots

items.head: What it is
items.body: A QR code is a square pattern of black and white dots that serves as a form of barcode: a camera reads it and recovers the text it stores. The book's first chapter describes the code shown on the receive screen of Alice's wallet in this way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: How it works
items.body: What a QR code stores is a string of characters, and the same text can be packed more or less densely.

slides.notes:
The code removes the need to type or to copy a long, easily mistyped string, and works between two devices that are not connected to each other at all, just a screen and a camera. For merchants it is the cheapest possible point of sale: a display and a printed or on-screen code. The chapter relies on it when Bob's system creates a QR code that contains an invoice, which Alice scans with her smartphone (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A QR code is not secure in itself. What is displayed is whatever someone chose to print, and a printed code that is covered by another one would replace the address without any visible sign. Check the address and the amount that your wallet decodes before you approve the payment, and the book's own tip about the chapter's code is to try to scan it with your wallet to see the address and amount, but not to send money (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Bitcoin improvement proposal
slides.sub: BIP 21 proposes the bitcoin: URI scheme

items.head: What it is
items.body: A Bitcoin improvement proposal, abbreviated BIP, is a design document that provides information to the Bitcoin community or describes a new feature for Bitcoin or its processes or environment.

rows: hdr = '  BIP: 21\n  Title: URI Scheme\n  Status: Closed'
dict(l.strip().split(': ', 1) for l in hdr.splitlines() if ': ' in l)['Status']

items.head: How it works
items.body: Each BIP begins with a header that gives its number, title, authors, status and type.

slides.notes:
Bitcoin has no company that decides how it changes. The BIP process gives the community a public and traceable way to propose changes and record the reasoning. BIP 1 states that the author of a BIP is responsible for building consensus within the community and documenting dissenting opinions, and that because BIPs are maintained as text files in a versioned repository, their revision history is the historical record of the feature proposal (Taaki, 2011). A BIP is not law: a standards track BIP matters only if the software and its users adopt it.

A proposal is not a decision. Many BIPs are never adopted, and a status such as proposed or draft says nothing about use. Status also changes: the BIP that the book cites for the invoice format, number 21, is no longer the current document, because it was replaced by a newer one that adds modern address types, and the book's reference is therefore a snapshot of 2023 (Corallo, 2024). Always check the status of the document you cite.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: BIP21 URI
slides.sub: the invoice encoded in the store's QR code

items.head: What it is
items.body: A BIP21 URI is a Bitcoin payment request written as a web link in the format defined by BIP 21.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The URI can be taken apart with the standard library. Splitting off the query and parsing it, then percent-decoding the label, returns Bob's Store, since %27 is the apostrophe and %20 a space.

slides.notes:
The format lets a wallet fill in a payment from a single scan and show the payer what is being paid for. The standard says the amount, if given, must be written in decimal bitcoin, with a period as the decimal separator, that the label and message are texts, and that clients must not act on such a URI without getting the user's authorization (Schneider and Corallo, 2012). The separation of address from description also keeps personal information out of the payment: the standard's rationale is that a URI should not represent an exchange of personal information, but a one-time payment (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

The invoice in the book is an illustration, not a record of the real payment. The amount 0.01577764 bitcoin is 1,577,764 satoshis, while the real transaction pays 75,000 satoshis to Bob's store, and the 22-byte output script of the real payment holds a different 20-byte program than the one encoded in the invoice's address. Do not conclude from the book's figures that the address in the URI received the payment. The book's own tip says to try scanning the code, but do not send money (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Bitcoin address and Exchange rate

items.head: Bitcoin address
items.body: A Bitcoin address is a short string of letters and digits that stands for the condition under which a payment can later be spent.
The newer format is readable in three parts.

items.head: Exchange rate
items.body: An exchange rate is the price of one unit of a currency expressed in another currency. In this chapter it is the number that turns a price in United States dollars into an amount of bitcoin.
The arithmetic is a division.

slides.notes:
An address exists for the payer's convenience and safety. A payer does not need to know anything about scripts, keys or hashes; the wallet turns the address into the output script that encumbers the payment, and the checksum inside the address catches a mistyped character before any money moves. The book makes the consequence explicit: the checksum prevents a mistyped address from being accepted by the wallet software as a valid destination, an error that would otherwise result in loss of funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

An address is not an account and not an identity. It holds no balance of its own, since a balance is the sum of the unspent outputs that a wallet can spend, and it names no person, which is why following a chain of transactions does not by itself reveal who the parties were. Addresses are also meant to be used once: the book explains that a change address is usually a new address of the sender's wallet for privacy reasons (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Finally, the address in the book's invoice is an illustration: a check of the real transaction shows that its payment output encodes a different twenty-byte program, so the printed address did not receive the printed payment.

---

The rate is where Bitcoin meets the ordinary economy, and it explains a figure that otherwise looks arbitrary. The amount in the invoice, 0.01577764 bitcoin, is not a round number because it is the dollar price of the podcast episode converted at the rate of that moment. It also explains why a merchant who quotes in a local currency carries no currency risk on the listed price while a merchant who quotes in bitcoin does. The chapter earlier notes that people accept a money only if they expect to be able to spend it later, which is a statement about value over time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A rate is a market price at an instant, and it is the one number in a payment request that goes stale. An invoice that was correct when it was displayed may be worth more or less a few minutes later, which is why merchants normally let a quoted bitcoin amount expire. The rate is also not part of Bitcoin: no rule of the protocol knows about dollars, and the figures printed in the book are a snapshot of 2023. Treat a rate as context for reading the chapter's amounts, never as a constant.

slides.title: Construction

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Construction is the work of turning a decision to pay into a valid transaction. In the chapter this is done entirely by Alice's wallet application, which contains all the logic for selecting inputs and generating outputs to build a transaction to Alice's specification (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group describes what the wallet does, in the order in which it does it: find inputs that can pay, create outputs, add a fee and sign.
The wallet starts from the outputs it controls, which it tracks.

slides.notes:
Construction is where the abstract parts of the first groups come together. A user sees only a destination, an amount and a fee; everything else, from the choice of inputs to the change, is a decision of the software. Understanding it explains why two wallets can build different transactions for the same payment, and why a wallet bug can lose money.

The wallet is trusted with decisions the user never sees, so the user must trust its code. That is why the book recommends a design in which wallets are open and reviewed, and why this course returns to wallets in a later chapter. The wallet cannot be trusted to know what has happened on the network if it is offline, either: a transaction built offline is only a candidate until it is sent.

Concepts in this section: Transaction construction, Wallet.

slides.title: Transaction construction and Wallet

items.head: Transaction construction
items.body: Constructing a transaction means assembling its inputs and outputs and signing it.

The sums can be rehearsed. With an input of 100000 satoshis, a payment of 75000 and a fee of 5000, the change is 100000 - 75000 - 5000, which is 20000, and the two output amounts are 20000 and 75000, exactly the amounts of Alice's real transaction.

items.head: Wallet
items.body: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin.
The arithmetic a wallet performs for a payment is the subtraction of this chapter.

slides.notes:
A transaction that has been constructed contains, in the words of the book, everything necessary to confirm ownership of the funds and assign new owners, so it can be sent to the network by any route (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is a major reason why Bitcoin needs no trusted intermediary: the proof of authorization travels inside the transaction, and nodes do not need to know who built it or how it reached them.

Four cautions follow. A wallet that has no knowledge of the current state of the network may build a transaction whose inputs have already been spent. A fee that is chosen too low may make the payment wait, and one that is chosen far too high is paid to the miner without any warning from the format. The signature covers the transaction as built, so a wallet cannot adjust the amounts after signing. And, the book adds, a wallet running on a lightweight client has less information than one running on a full node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

---

The wallet is where all the complexity of the chapter is hidden from the user. The book says that Alice's wallet application contains all the logic for selecting inputs and generating outputs to build a transaction to her specification, and that she only needs to choose a destination, an amount and a transaction fee while the rest happens without her seeing the details (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Everything a reader has met so far, coin selection, change, fees, scripts and signatures, is a decision that this program makes, which is why trusting a wallet is as consequential as trusting a bank used to be.

A wallet does not contain bitcoins. It contains keys and a view of the ledger, which is why a backup of the keys restores the funds and a copy of the balance does not. Two further cautions belong here. A wallet that is offline cannot know whether an output it believes it controls has already been spent, so a transaction built offline is only a candidate until the network accepts it. And the user cannot see what the wallet decided, so a defect in the software can overpay a fee or leak a change address without any warning; the book's chapter on fees asks wallets to make an excessive fee rate hard to pay by accident (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Network
slides.sub: The Bitcoin network is the set of computers that run the Bitcoin protocol and exchange transactions and blocks with one another. This second branch of the chapter follows Alice's transaction out of her wallet and across that network.
slides.notes:
The branch matters because the network is what makes the system work without a company in the middle. There is no server that collects payments and no directory that decides who may take part, so a transaction reaches the miners only because independent computers pass it on, and each of them checks it first. That is also what makes the network robust: the chapter notes that it does not matter how or where a transaction is transmitted, since the transaction contains everything necessary for it to be processed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Any route will do, and no single point can block a payment.

Three cautions apply throughout the branch. Reaching the network is not the same as being recorded: the chapter is careful to say that a transaction does not become part of the blockchain until it is included in a block, which belongs to the next branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Being received by many nodes is not a vote either, since each node decides for itself by the rules. And a peer is not a trusted party: everything that arrives from one is checked, which is exactly why a node can safely connect to strangers.

slides.title: Who takes part

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: This group names the kinds of program that make up the network and says what each of them can and cannot check. The chapter introduces them in one passage: peers in the Bitcoin peer-to-peer network are programs that have both the software logic and the data necessary to fully verify the correctness of a new transaction, that the connections between peers are often drawn as the edges of a graph whose nodes are the peers themselves, and that for that reason Bitcoin peers are commonly called full verification nodes, or full nodes for short (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The group has four concepts, from the most capable to the most abstract. The full node verifies every rule and keeps the data needed to do so.

slides.notes:
The distinctions in this group decide whom a user has to trust. A program that verifies every rule for itself needs to trust nobody; a program that asks others for answers has to trust what it is told, at least in part. The chapter uses exactly this difference when it describes Bob's situation: his wallet can verify that Alice's transaction is well formed, but only if Bob is using his own full node can his wallet further verify that the transaction spends valid unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same difference runs through the rest of the course.

Resist two tidy pictures. The first is that these kinds are sharp: the book's network chapter explains that a full node may also carry routing, mining and wallet functions, and that some nodes keep a complete archival copy while others do not, so the roles overlap (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is that more participants automatically means more security; what matters is how many independently verify the rules, which is why this group separates the counting of nodes from the question of what each of them actually checks.

Concepts in this section: Full node, Lightweight client, Peer and connection, Peer-to-peer network.

slides.title: Full node
slides.sub: a program that verifies every rule

items.head: What it is
items.body: A full node, which the chapter calls a full verification node, is a program that has both the software logic and the data necessary to fully verify the correctness of a new transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

rows: checks = {'syntax': True, 'inputs_nonempty': True, 'amounts_in_range': True, 'outputs_unspent': True, 'scripts_valid': True}

items.head: How it works
items.body: Verification is the running of a checklist.

slides.notes:
