The full node is the reason the chapter can open by saying that the Bitcoin system does not require trust in third parties, and that each user can run software on their own computer to verify the correct operation of every aspect of the system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A user with a full node accepts a payment because their own program checked it; a user without one accepts it because somebody else said so. The book adds that running a full node gives the pure Bitcoin experience, independent verification of all transactions without the need to rely on, or trust, any other system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A full node is not a miner and not a wallet, although one program may do all three. It also does not make a user anonymous or protect their keys, and it does not remove every trust: a user still trusts the software they downloaded, which is why the next chapter of the course is about verifying a release of Bitcoin Core. Finally, a node's view can be briefly out of date, since it learns of a new block only when a peer sends it; what it never does is accept a block or transaction that breaks a rule it enforces.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Lightweight client and Peer and connection

items.head: Lightweight client
items.body: A lightweight client is a Bitcoin program that does not verify everything.
The saving comes from the size of a header.

items.head: Peer and connection
items.body: A peer is another participant of the network with which a node maintains a connection in order to exchange transactions and blocks.
A connection is a link between two nodes over which messages travel, and a node has several at once; the small example counts a set of three and names the first.

slides.notes:
Lightweight clients exist because verification costs resources that a telephone does not have. The book says they are designed to run on space- and power-constrained devices such as smartphones, tablets and embedded systems (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The trade is explicit: the client gets a usable wallet in a pocket and gives up the ability to check everything for itself, relying instead on peers to provide partial views of the relevant parts of the blockchain on demand (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Knowing which of the two kinds a wallet is tells a user exactly how much of the chapter's guarantee applies to them.

A lightweight client cannot tell by itself whether a transaction obeys the rules; it can only see that it was committed to by work. The book's comparison is a tourist with a street map against a tourist asking strangers for directions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). There is a privacy cost as well, since asking peers which transactions concern you tells them which transactions concern you, and the book devotes a section to that problem (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's warning about block explorers is the same point in another form: looking something up may tell the operator what you are interested in (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

---

Peers are how a node learns anything at all. There is no server to ask, so every unconfirmed transaction and every new block reaches a node from a peer, and everything the node has accepted is passed on to its peers in turn. The word also carries a claim about equality: because the participants are of the same kind, no one of them can be removed to stop the network, and the chapter can say that it does not matter how or where a transaction is transmitted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For an operator, each connection is also a small cost in memory and bandwidth.

A peer is not a trusted party, and this is the single most important thing to remember about the word. Everything a peer sends is checked against the rules by the receiving node, which is why connecting to unknown computers is safe for the data. The number of peers is also not a measure of correctness, and a node that is connected to many peers still accepts only what passes its own checks. Finally, peers see what you send them: the book's chapter on lightweight clients and privacy explains that what a program asks its peers for can reveal what it is interested in (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Peer-to-peer network

items.head: What it is
items.body: A peer-to-peer network, often abbreviated to P2P, is a network in which the participants are equals: each of them performs the same functions, each both provides and consumes services, and none of them is special.
What makes the structure work is that every node keeps several connections, so that the whole is connected without any central point.

slides.notes:
For Bitcoin the architecture is not a technical preference but a consequence of the goal. The book writes that Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer digital cash system by design, that the network architecture is both a reflection and a foundation of that characteristic, and that decentralization of control can only be achieved and maintained by a flat and decentralized consensus network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nakamoto's paper is titled for the same idea and proposes a solution using a peer-to-peer network in which the participants timestamp transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of proof of work (Nakamoto, 2008). If there were a server, whoever ran it could decide what counts as a payment.

Peer-to-peer does not mean that every participant does the same amount of work, nor that there are no services built on top. The book notes that beside the base protocol there are others used for mining and for lightweight wallets, provided by gateway servers that bridge into the peer-to-peer network, and that various companies run nodes as network edge routers on which exchanges, wallets, explorers and payment processors are built (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Those services are centralized even though the protocol beneath them is not, and a user who relies on one of them is relying on its operator.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Propagation

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Propagation is the spreading of a transaction or a block from the computer that first has it to the rest of the network. This group follows Alice's payment through that spreading, from the moment her wallet transmits it to the moment a reader can look it up from outside.
The group is taken in the order of the journey. Transmission is the first hop out of the wallet.

slides.notes:
The group explains why a payment can be trusted within seconds even though it is not yet recorded. Each node that forwards the transaction has first verified it, so propagation is not mere copying: it is a wave of independent checks. That is also the reason the chapter can say that invalid data does not travel far, and the reason a merchant may make a judgement about an unconfirmed payment, as the security group of the next branch discusses.

Propagation proves nothing about permanence. A transaction that has reached every node is still unconfirmed, can still be replaced in some circumstances, and is recorded only when a miner includes it in a block that other nodes accept. Speed can also mislead: that a payment appeared in a wallet within two seconds says only that the data arrived, not that the money cannot be taken back, which is the subject of the confirmation concept in the next branch.

Concepts in this section: Transmitting the transaction, Gossiping, Transaction propagation, Memory pool, The recipient's own check, Block explorer.

slides.title: Transmitting the transaction and Gossiping

items.head: Transmitting the transaction
items.body: Transmission is the step in which a finished, signed transaction leaves the wallet that built it and is handed to the network.

items.head: Gossiping
items.body: Gossiping is the name the chapter gives to the way data spreads through the Bitcoin network.
The reach grows multiplicatively.

slides.notes:
This indifference to the route is one of Bitcoin's quietly radical properties. A payment is not a request sent to an institution that may accept or refuse it; it is a self-contained document whose validity any recipient can check. The chapter draws out the practical consequences: Alice's wallet can send the transaction to any Bitcoin node over any type of connection, wired, wireless or mobile, and it can also send it to another program, such as a block explorer, that will relay it to a node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Her wallet does not have to be connected to Bob's wallet directly, and she does not have to use the internet connection offered by Bob, though both of those are possible as well.

Two things are not guaranteed by transmission. The first is arrival: a wallet that sends a transaction to a single node and gets no acknowledgement does not know that the network has it, which is why wallets usually send to several peers and watch for the transaction coming back to them. The second is acceptance: a node that finds the transaction invalid simply drops it, and the chapter's rule is that a node forwards a valid transaction it has not seen before (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Relaying through a third party such as an explorer also tells that party who is paying whom, which is the privacy cost the chapter warns of.

---

Gossiping is how a network with no coordinator reaches everybody. Nobody holds a list of participants and nobody decides the route, yet the chapter can say that the transaction rapidly propagates out across the peer-to-peer network, reaching a large percentage of the nodes within a few seconds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The validity condition is what makes this safe rather than reckless: the book's mining chapter explains that every node verifies a transaction before forwarding it, so that only valid transactions are propagated while invalid ones are discarded at the first node that encounters them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Gossiping does not guarantee that every node will hold a given transaction. A node may be offline, may have a full memory pool, or may apply its own relay policy, and the book's chapter on fees notes that nodes limit how many unconfirmed transactions they store (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nor does gossiping record anything: the data is in memory, not in the blockchain. And because what spreads is what a node has accepted, a transaction that one node's policy rejects may travel less widely without being invalid, so wide propagation is evidence of acceptance rather than proof of it.

slides.title: Transaction propagation and Memory pool

items.head: Transaction propagation
items.body: Transaction propagation is the spread of a signed transaction across the network until it has reached, in practice, everyone who cares, including the miners who may record it.
The rough arithmetic of the chapter's claim can be done.

items.head: Memory pool
items.body: The memory pool, usually shortened to mempool, is the collection of transactions that a node has verified but that are not yet in any block.

rows: [t for t in pool if t not in mined]

items.body: Maintaining the pool is adding and removing.

slides.notes:
Propagation is the step that turns a private document into public knowledge, and it is what makes the double-spend check meaningful. If every node sees the transaction that spends an output, a second transaction spending the same output will be rejected by the nodes that already hold the first, so a fraudulent payment has to beat the honest one through the network. Propagation is also what the receiver relies on in the first seconds: before any block exists, the only evidence Bob has is that his own program and everybody else's have seen the payment and found it valid.

Propagation is not confirmation, and this is the misconception the chapter is most careful about: a transaction does not become part of the blockchain until it is included in a block by mining and that block has been validated by full nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A widely propagated transaction can still be dropped if it is never mined, and in some circumstances it can be replaced by another version paying a higher fee, which the book's chapter on fees describes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). What propagation gives is visibility and a first, probabilistic assurance, nothing more.

---

The pool is the waiting room of the system, and it is where the market for block space happens. A miner builds a candidate block out of the pool, and the chapter says that transactions are added to the new block prioritized by the highest fee rate first and a few other criteria (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), so the pool is what the fee rate concept is about. For a user, the pool explains the state a payment is in during the first minutes: verified by everyone, recorded by nobody.

The memory pool is local, not global. The book is explicit that the memory pool and the orphan pool represent a single node's local perspective and might vary significantly from node to node depending on when the node was started or restarted, unlike the database of unspent outputs, which represents the emergent consensus of the network and will not usually vary (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). So there is no such thing as the mempool, only each node's own; a transaction in your node's pool may be missing from another's, and nothing in the pool is recorded until it is mined.

slides.title: The recipient's own check

items.head: What it is
items.body: The recipient's own check is what happens in Bob's wallet when Alice's transaction arrives. The chapter devotes a short section to it, called Bob's view, and makes three statements.

rows: [i for i, (amt, owner) in enumerate(outs) if owner == mine]

items.head: How it works
items.body: Recognition is a search through the outputs for one that the wallet's own keys can spend.

slides.notes:
This concept is where the chapter's opening promise becomes concrete for a particular person. Bob does not have to telephone a bank or trust Alice: his own program reads the transaction and recognises the payment. The three statements also form a ladder of assurance that the course returns to again and again. Recognising an output addressed to oneself requires nothing but one's own keys; checking that the data is well formed requires only the rules of the format; checking that the inputs exist and are unspent requires the whole ledger, which is what a full node has.

What the recipient's check cannot establish is that the payment is final. The transaction is unconfirmed at this point, so the assurance is about validity, not permanence, and the chapter moves straight on to mining for that reason. A lightweight wallet is also limited in a way its user may not notice: it will show the incoming payment, but it has not verified that the inputs were unspent, so it is trusting its peers for that part. And recognising an output as one's own is not the same as being able to spend it yet, since an output in an unconfirmed transaction can only be spent further once there is something to build on.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Block explorer
slides.sub: a web page showing Alice's transaction

items.head: What it is
items.body: A block explorer is a web application that operates as a Bitcoin search engine: it allows you to search for addresses, transactions and blocks and to see the relationships and flows between them, in the chapter's own words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

rows: 'txid' if len(q) == 64 else 'address' if q.startswith('bc1') else 'height'

items.body: An explorer works out from the shape of the query what is being asked for, and the small example shows the idea: a query of sixty-four hexadecimal characters is a transaction or block hash, a string beginning with bc1 is an address of the newer format, and a plain number is a block height.

slides.notes:
The explorer is what makes this chapter checkable by a reader who has no node. All the data in the blockchain is public, but reading it from the network requires software and a copy of the chain; an explorer does that work and presents the result as a web page. For a course it is also the simplest instrument of the subject: a student can see a real input pointing at a real earlier output, and watch a transaction move from unconfirmed to one confirmation and then to more.

The chapter attaches a warning to the explorer and so should the reader. Searching information on a block explorer may disclose to its operator that you are interested in that information, allowing them to associate it with your address on the internet, your browser details, your past searches or other identifiable information; looking up the transactions in the book is harmless, but looking up your own may let the operator guess how many bitcoins you have received, spent and currently own (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). An explorer is also a third party: what it shows has not been verified by you, which is exactly the trust that running a full node removes.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Blockchain
slides.sub: The blockchain is the record in which Bitcoin's transactions are finally written down.
slides.notes:
The branch answers the question that the first two leave open. A transaction that every node has seen and found valid is still only a proposal: nothing yet says that this payment, and not a competing one spending the same output, is the one that counts. The chapter's answer is computation. Bitcoin's system of counterfeit protection is based on computation: transactions are bundled into blocks whose headers must be formed in a very specific way, requiring an enormous amount of computation to get right but only a small amount to verify as correct (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That asymmetry is what replaces the authority of a bank.

Two habits of language should be corrected early. First, a block is not added by anybody's decision: a miner publishes a candidate that satisfies the rules, and each node decides for itself whether to accept it, which the book calls independent validation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Second, nothing in Bitcoin is final in the absolute sense; the book writes that while the protocol always allows a chain to be undone by a longer chain, the probability of such an event decreases as time passes until it becomes infinitesimal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The security of this branch is probabilistic, and saying so precisely is part of understanding it.

slides.title: Mining

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Mining is the process that turns a pool of unconfirmed transactions into the next block of the blockchain.
The group is taken in the order in which a block is built. The miner is the specialized node that does the work. The candidate block is what it assembles from its memory pool.

slides.notes:
The group explains Bitcoin's answer to a problem that has no obvious solution: how a network of strangers can agree on an order of events without a referee. The chapter names the two purposes that mining serves. Miners can only receive honest income from creating blocks that follow all of Bitcoin's consensus rules, so they are normally incentivized to include only valid transactions, which allows users to make a trust-based assumption that any transaction in a block is valid; and mining currently creates new bitcoins in each block, almost like a central bank printing new money, in an amount that is limited and diminishes with time following a fixed issuance schedule (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Three warnings belong to the whole group. Mining does not verify transactions on behalf of the network: every full node verifies for itself, and mining decides only the order and the timing. The ten-minute figure is an average and not a schedule, which the security group takes up. And the figures of this group, the reward, the hash rate and the difficulty, change continuously; what is stable is the rule that produces them, so a learner should remember the rule and look up the number.

Concepts in this section: Miner, Candidate block, Proof of work, Block, Block header, Merkle tree, Difficulty and target, Hash rate, Consensus rules, Coinbase transaction, Block reward, Mining pool, Sudoku analogy, Soft fork and hard fork.

slides.title: Miner and Candidate block

items.head: Miner
items.body: A miner is a participant that builds candidate blocks and searches for the proof of work that would make one of them valid.
A miner's income is a sum of two parts.

items.head: Candidate block
items.body: A candidate block is the block a miner is working on: the transactions it wants to include, a commitment to the previous block, and the other header fields, assembled but without a valid proof of work.
Assembling a candidate is selection plus commitment.

slides.notes:
Miners exist because somebody has to decide the order of transactions, and Bitcoin pays for that service instead of appointing anybody to it. The chapter describes the balance: mining uses electricity to solve a computational problem, a successful miner collects a reward in the form of new bitcoins and transaction fees, but the reward will only be collected if the miner has included only valid transactions, with the rules for consensus determining what is valid, and this delicate balance provides security for Bitcoin without a central authority (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A miner cannot cheat by writing itself a larger reward. The book puts the question directly and answers it: an inflated reward would make the block invalid in the eyes of everyone else, wasting the electricity spent on the proof of work, because the miner only gets to spend the reward if the block is accepted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nor is a miner a judge of transactions: it chooses which valid transactions to include, usually by fee rate, but it cannot make an invalid one valid. And mining is not a vote of users: it counts computation, and the nodes that enforce the rules decide what they will accept.

---

The candidate block is where a miner's choices are made, and therefore where the market for block space is settled. The chapter says that transactions are added to the new block prioritized by the highest fee rate transactions first and a few other criteria, and that each miner starts the process of mining a new candidate block as soon as they receive the previous block from the network, knowing that some other miner won that iteration of the lottery (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The candidate is also the lottery ticket in the chapter's own image: each miner can create their own ticket by creating a candidate block that includes the new transactions they want to mine plus some additional data fields (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A candidate block is not a block: it has no proof of work, so no node would accept it, and the miner may abandon it at any moment. It is also private until it is solved, which is why two miners can be working on candidates that contain the same transactions without any conflict. And the contents of a candidate are a choice, not a rule: a miner may legally build a block with no transactions at all except the coinbase, which is one of the problems the book describes on the test network, where fees have no value (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Proof of work
slides.sub: a header hash below the target

items.head: What it is
items.body: Proof of work is a piece of data that takes a great deal of computation to find and almost none to check.

rows: next(n for n in range(200000) if h(('1' + str(n) + 'Alice pays Bob 75000').encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0000'))

items.head: How it works
items.body: The search is a loop with one changing field.

slides.notes:
Proof of work is what makes the record expensive to rewrite, and therefore what makes a confirmed payment reliable. The chapter puts the number on it: as of writing, the number of candidate blocks miners need to try before finding a winning combination is about 168 billion trillion, and that is also how many times the hash function needs to be run; yet once a winning combination has been found, anyone can verify the block is valid by running the hash function just once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Changing a recorded transaction would mean redoing that work and then outpacing everyone else, which is the argument the security group develops.

Proof of work proves effort, not honesty and not truth. A block with a perfect proof of work is still rejected if any of its transactions breaks a rule, as the consensus-rules concept explains. The proof is also probabilistic: the chapter's own wording is that the verification process is able to probabilistically prove the work was done, and a lucky miner may find a solution on its first attempt (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Finally, the work is not a puzzle with a meaningful answer; the solution has no use outside the system, which is both the source of its security and the reason its energy cost is debated.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Block
slides.sub: a header plus a list of transactions

items.head: What it is
items.body: A block is the unit in which transactions are added to the blockchain.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The proportions are worth remembering.

slides.notes:
The block is what gives transactions an order and a time. Within a single chain of blocks the position of a transaction defines whether it is earlier or later than another, and a transaction is valid only if it spends outputs of transactions that appeared earlier, which the book says eliminates the problem of double spending (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The block is also the unit in which block space is sold, so its limit is what makes fees necessary, and the unit in which security accumulates, since confirmations are counted in blocks.

Two points are easily confused. A block is not a fixed number of transactions: the limit is on size, counted as weight, so a block may hold one transaction or many thousands. And the hash that names a block is not stored inside it; the book notes that the block's hash is computed by each node as the block is received from the network, which is why every node can check the name for itself and nobody can rename a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Block header

items.head: What it is
items.body: The block header is the small, fixed part of a block that carries its metadata and that mining actually works on.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The header can be assembled and hashed with the standard library, which is the executed example of this concept.

slides.notes:
Everything the chapter claims about the chain follows from this header. Because the header contains the hash of the parent block, any change to a parent requires the child's hash to change, which requires the grandchild to change, and so on; the book concludes that once a block has many generations following it, it cannot be changed without forcing a recalculation of all subsequent blocks, and that because such a recalculation would require enormous computation, the existence of a long chain of blocks makes the blockchain's deep history impractical to change, which is a key feature of Bitcoin's security (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because the header also contains the merkle root, it commits to every transaction without containing any of them.

Three cautions. The header's version field is no longer simply a version, as the book says its use has evolved over time, and the chapter on Bitcoin Core explains how it came to carry signals for upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The timestamp is the approximate creation time, set by the miner within limits that the book states as two consensus rules, that no node accepts a block whose time is more than two hours in the future and none accepts a block whose time is not later than the median time of the last eleven blocks, which the book calls the median time past, so a block's time is not a reliable clock (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the nonce is only four bytes, so it is exhausted quickly; miners then change other fields, which the book calls the extra nonce solution (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Merkle tree
slides.sub: four transactions summarised in one hash

items.head: What it is
items.body: A merkle tree, also called a binary hash tree, is a structure for summarizing and verifying the integrity of large sets of data.

rows: L = [d(x) for x in (b'A', b'B', b'C', b'D')]

items.head: How it works
items.body: The construction is a few lines of code, and the executed example performs it.

slides.notes:
The tree is what lets the eighty-byte header stand for a whole block. The book says that merkle trees are used in Bitcoin to summarize all the transactions in a block, producing an overall commitment to the entire set of transactions and permitting a very efficient process to verify whether a transaction is included in a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also gives the efficiency: with N elements, checking whether any one of them is in the tree takes about the base-two logarithm of N calculations, so proving that one transaction out of the roughly sixteen thousand in the largest possible block is present needs the transaction, the eighty-byte header and 448 bytes of path, which makes the largest possible proof almost ten thousand times smaller than the largest possible block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The merkle root commits to the transactions but does not contain them, so a header alone does not let anyone read a block. A merkle path also proves only inclusion: it shows that a transaction is in a block, not that the transaction or the block obeys the rules, which is exactly the limit of simplified payment verification. And the chapter's own text never mentions merkle trees; the concept is brought in here because the chapter's claim that a small header commits to many transactions cannot otherwise be explained.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Difficulty and target

items.head: What it is
items.body: The target is the number that a block header's hash must be below for the block to be valid, and the difficulty is the inverse way of describing the same thing: the book's glossary calls difficulty a network-wide setting that controls how much computation is required to produce a proof of work, and the difficulty target a difficulty at which all the computation in the network will find blocks approximately every ten minutes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The compact form packs an exponent and a coefficient into four bytes.

slides.notes:
Without an adjustable target the system would not keep time. The book explains that blocks are generated every ten minutes on average, that this is Bitcoin's heartbeat and underpins the frequency of currency issuance and the speed of transaction settlement, and that it has to remain constant over decades while computer power and the number of miners change, so the difficulty of mining must be adjusted to account for those changes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter touches the same idea when it says that over time, as the height of new blocks increases, so does the computation difficulty for the chain as a whole (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Three details are often got wrong. Retargeting is not performed by anybody: it occurs automatically and on every node independently, which is why all nodes agree on the result (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The window has an off-by-one error that the book records, since the calculation uses the time of the previous 2,015 blocks rather than 2,016, biasing difficulty upward by about 0.05 per cent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the target is independent of how many transactions a block holds or how much value they move, so the energy spent securing Bitcoin does not depend on how much Bitcoin is used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Hash rate
slides.sub: hashes per second across the network

items.head: What it is
items.body: The hash rate is the speed at which hash computations are performed, counted in hashes per second. It is the natural measure of mining effort, because mining is nothing but repeated hashing, and it is used both for a single machine and for the network as a whole.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The network's rate follows from the chapter's own number by one division.

slides.notes:
The hash rate is how the cost of rewriting history is quantified, so it is the number behind every security claim in this branch. The book's note on block intervals makes the link: a malicious miner wanting to double spend a transaction would need to do an amount of work equal to ten minutes of the total network hash rate in order to create a chain with equal proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A share of the hash rate is also what defines the attacks the book describes, which it calls hashrate attacks and which succeed with probability depending on that share (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A hash rate is an estimate, not a measurement: nobody counts the hashes of the world's miners, so the figure is inferred from the difficulty and the observed block times, which is why published values differ and fluctuate. It also measures only this one kind of computation, so comparing it with the speed of a general-purpose computer is meaningless. And a higher network hash rate does not make payments faster; the difficulty adjusts to keep the pace at ten minutes, so extra hash rate buys security, not speed.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Consensus rules
slides.sub: the checks every block must pass

items.head: What it is
items.body: The consensus rules are the rules by which a full node decides whether a block and the transactions in it are acceptable.

rows: rules = {'pow_below_target': True, 'first_tx_is_coinbase': True, 'weight_within_limits': True, 'timestamp_in_range': True, 'all_txs_valid': True}

items.body: Validation is the conjunction of independent checks, which the small example renders as a set of five that must all hold; the count is how many were applied and the verdict is whether every one passed. The order matters in practice, since cheap checks come first, but logically a block is valid only if nothing fails.

slides.notes:
The rules are what makes a decentralized record possible at all. Because every node applies the same rules, no miner can profit from breaking them: the book explains that an invalid coinbase transaction would make the entire block invalid, so the block would be rejected and the transaction would never become part of the blockchain, and that the miners therefore have to construct a block based on the shared rules that all nodes follow and mine it with a correct solution, expending electricity that is wasted if they cheat (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter draws the consequence for users: because miners are incentivized to include only valid transactions, users may optionally make a trust-based assumption that any transaction in a block is a valid transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Consensus rules are not the same as consensus, and the book warns against confusing the two: the rules are what nodes check, while consensus is the agreement that results (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The rules also change, but only in careful ways: the book devotes a long section to how they are altered, distinguishing a soft fork, which tightens them compatibly, from a hard fork, which does not (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the rules are enforced by nodes, not by miners; a block with a perfect proof of work that breaks a rule is simply discarded.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Coinbase transaction and Block reward

items.head: Coinbase transaction
items.body: The coinbase transaction is the special first transaction of every block, by which the miner pays itself.

items.head: Block reward
items.body: The block reward is what a miner earns for a block: the newly created bitcoins, which the book calls the subsidy, together with the transaction fees of everything in the block.
The rule is a halving, which in whole numbers is a right shift.

slides.notes:
This transaction is where new bitcoins enter the world, so it is the only place in the system where money is created rather than moved. It is also what ties the miner's income to the validity of the whole block: the fees it claims are the differences between the inputs and outputs of the other transactions, so an error anywhere in the block makes the coinbase transaction wrong and the block invalid. The chapter's statement that a successful miner receives the reward after the block is added to the blockchain and the reward transaction becomes spendable refers to this transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Three traps. The output of a coinbase transaction cannot be spent immediately: the book's verification checklist requires at least a hundred confirmations, the constant it calls COINBASE_MATURITY, and its blockchain chapter explains that after a hundred blocks there is so much stability that the reward can be spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The term is also overloaded: the glossary warns that the coinbase, a field, is not to be confused with the coinbase transaction, and neither has anything to do with a company of a similar name (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Finally, the miner cannot write any amount it likes, because every node recomputes the permitted total.

---

The reward is the engine of the whole system. It pays for the computation that secures the record, and because it diminishes on a schedule that nobody can change, it also defines Bitcoin's monetary policy. The book draws the conclusion: the finite and diminishing issuance creates a fixed monetary supply that resists inflation, and unlike a fiat currency, which can be printed in infinite numbers by a central bank, no individual party has the ability to inflate the supply (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also tells the miner's future: after the subsidy reaches zero, blocks will contain no new bitcoins and miners will be rewarded solely through transaction fees (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Any particular reward figure goes stale, so learn the rule and not the number; the book's own glossary still says the reward is currently 12.5 bitcoins, which was true two halvings earlier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Note also that the maximum is an upper limit rather than a promise: the book remarks that a miner may intentionally mine a block taking less than the full reward, and that such blocks have already been mined, so the total issued may end up lower (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the reward is not paid immediately in a usable form, because the coinbase output must mature for a hundred blocks.

slides.title: Mining pool
slides.sub: many small miners sharing one reward

items.head: What it is
items.body: A mining pool is an arrangement in which many miners search for the same block together and share whatever is found.

rows: {m: reward * s // sum(shares.values()) for m, s in shares.items()}

items.head: How it works
items.body: The pool measures contributions with Bitcoin's own proof of work at an easier setting.

slides.notes:
Pools exist because mining alone has become a lottery with very long odds. The book says that in this highly competitive environment individual miners working alone do not stand a chance, that the likelihood of finding a block to offset electricity and hardware costs is so low that it represents a gamble, and that by participating in a pool miners get a smaller share of the overall reward but typically get rewarded every day, reducing uncertainty (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its example is concrete: a miner with a ten-thousandth of one per cent of the network's hash rate would find a block about once every twenty years alone, and in a pool holding one per cent of the rate would average more than one block a day and earn the same amount, only far more evenly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Pools change who controls what. A pool member runs the hardware but the pool decides what goes into the candidate block, so hash rate concentrates in the hands of pool operators, and the book's section on hashrate attacks notes that a pool with a large share can attempt them while its participants might remain blissfully unaware (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A share is also not a bitcoin: it is a unit of accounting inside the pool, worth nothing outside it. And a pool is a counterparty, so its members trust it to measure and to pay.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Sudoku analogy and Soft fork and hard fork

items.head: Sudoku analogy
items.body: The sudoku analogy is a teaching picture, taken from the owner's course notes for this chapter, in which mining is described as a giant competitive game of sudoku.
The comparison can be made quantitative, which is also where it breaks down.

items.head: Soft fork and hard fork
items.body: A rule change is an alteration of the consensus rules, and it comes in two kinds.

rows: 'soft fork' if new_valid <= old_valid else 'hard fork'

items.body: The test is a comparison of what each version of the rules accepts.

slides.notes:
The analogy is useful because it captures the one property that makes proof of work possible, the asymmetry between solving and checking, in an everyday object. A student who has filled in a sudoku knows from experience that finding the answer is laborious while checking a finished grid is quick, and that a larger grid is harder without being harder to check. Those are exactly the properties the chapter claims for the hash search: an enormous amount of computation to get right, only a small amount of computation to verify as correct (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The analogy must be labelled as one. A sudoku has a unique solution reached by reasoning, whereas a proof of work has very many possible solutions and no reasoning helps: the only method is trial, because the hash function's output cannot be steered. A sudoku also has no reward, no competition between solvers for the same grid and no chain of earlier grids, so the analogy says nothing about incentives, about confirmations or about why a long chain is hard to rewrite. Use it to understand the asymmetry and then put it down.

---

The distinction decides whether an upgrade can happen without splitting the network, so it is the practical reason Bitcoin can change at all. The book states the rule precisely: a soft fork is a forward-compatible change to the consensus rules that allows unupgraded clients to continue to operate in consensus with the new rules, and it adds the consequence that is not immediately obvious, that soft forks can only be used to constrain the consensus rules and not to expand them, because transactions and blocks created under the new rules must be valid under the old rules too but not the other way round (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Three cautions. The word fork here is not the accidental fork of the security group, which is two blocks at the same height, and the book remarks that in practice a soft fork is not a fork at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A soft fork is compatible but not free: an unupgraded node keeps accepting blocks yet no longer verifies the new rule itself, so a user who wants the new protection must upgrade. And compatibility is a property of the rules, not of intentions: a change that was meant to be gentle is still a hard fork if any old node would reject a block that a new one accepts.

slides.title: Security

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Security, in this chapter, means the confidence that a payment already recorded will stay recorded. This group collects the concepts that make that confidence precise.
The group is read from the unit upward.

slides.notes:
The group matters because the honest answer to the question is probabilistic, and students are owed the honest answer. The chapter does not say that a confirmed payment cannot be reversed; it says that as the blocks pile on top of each other it becomes harder to reverse the transaction, thereby giving Bob more and more confidence that Alice's payment is secure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The reason is an argument about cost: the chapter shows that a miner conspiring with Alice would have to produce two blocks where an honest miner produces one, and that the high cost of doing so for a small additional payment is normally much less profitable than honest mining (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Guard against two opposite errors. One is to treat six confirmations as a magic number: the chapter calls it a convention, and the book's own advice for high-value items is to wait longer, mentioning twenty-four hours, which is about 144 confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The other is to treat the system as fragile because nothing is absolute; the same arithmetic that denies certainty shows that the probability of reversal falls away very quickly, and the book's figure of a probability of about two in ten thousand after six confirmations against an attacker with a tenth of the hash rate is the concrete form of that (Nakamoto, 2008).

Concepts in this section: Confirmation, Probability of reversal, Best blockchain, Block height, Fork and alternative block, Double spend, Genesis block, Unconfirmed transaction, Accepting a small payment unconfirmed.

slides.title: Confirmation and Probability of reversal

items.head: Confirmation
items.body: A confirmation is a block that commits to a transaction, counted once for the block that contains it and once more for each block built on top.
The counting is addition, and the small example performs it: a transaction whose block has two blocks on top has three confirmations. The reason each one matters is the chain of header hashes.

items.head: Probability of reversal
items.body: The probability of reversal is the chance that a transaction already in the blockchain is removed, because somebody builds a competing chain that excludes it and that other nodes come to prefer.
Two calculations are worth doing.

slides.notes:
Confirmations are how the chapter turns a vague feeling of safety into a number that a merchant can act on. Each additional block multiplies the work an attacker would have to redo, because the attacker must not only replace the block containing the transaction but also outpace the honest chain that has grown in the meantime. The chapter spells the arithmetic out: after a second block is mined on top, Alice's transaction can only be changed if two alternative blocks are mined plus a new block on top of them, a total of three blocks, for Alice to take back the money she sent Bob (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A confirmation is not a guarantee and six is not a law. The chapter calls the six-block figure a convention, and the book's mining chapter describes a hashrate attack in which an attacker with enough power invalidates six or more blocks in a row, so that transactions considered immutable become invalid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the other direction, the number of confirmations says nothing about whether the transaction was correct, only about how hard it now is to remove; a payment to the wrong address is just as irreversible as a payment to the right one.

---

Without a number, the advice to wait for confirmations is folklore. With one, it becomes engineering: a merchant can weigh the value of the goods against the chance of losing them and choose how long to wait. The paper's own conclusion is the one the chapter repeats in words, that the probability of a successful attack drops exponentially as blocks are added, and that the receiver therefore becomes safer by waiting (Nakamoto, 2008). The book's blockchain chapter puts the same thing as a picture of geological layers, in which the topsoil may blow away while the deeper strata have been undisturbed for ages (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

These probabilities rest on assumptions, and the assumptions matter more than the digits. They assume the attacker has a minority of the hash rate, and the book's section on hashrate attacks shows that with a majority the arithmetic changes qualitatively, since success becomes almost certain given enough patience (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They also describe only this one attack: they say nothing about a stolen key, a faulty wallet or a payment sent to the wrong place, which are far more common ways to lose money than a reorganization of the chain.

slides.title: Best blockchain and Block height

items.head: Best blockchain
items.body: The best blockchain is the valid chain of blocks that carries the most cumulative proof of work, and it is the chain that a node treats as the record.
Choosing is comparing two sums. The small example models two chains by the work in each of their blocks and picks the one whose total is larger, which is chain B.

items.head: Block height
items.body: The height of a block is its position in the chain, counted as the number of blocks below it.

slides.notes:
This single rule is what produces agreement without agreement being negotiated. Every node applies it to the blocks it has, so nodes that have seen the same blocks reach the same conclusion, and nodes that have seen different blocks converge as soon as the missing blocks arrive. The book says so directly: by selecting the greatest-cumulative-work valid chain, all nodes eventually achieve network-wide consensus, and temporary discrepancies between chains are resolved eventually as more work is added (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is also the rule that sets the price of rewriting history, since an attacker must produce more work than everyone else combined over the period in question.

Three corrections to common wording. The rule is most work, not longest chain: a chain of fewer blocks mined at a higher difficulty can carry more work, which is why the book speaks of cumulative proof of work. The rule applies only among valid chains, so a chain with more work that breaks a rule is not a candidate at all. And the choice is each node's own, made independently; there is no vote and no announcement, which is exactly why no authority is needed.

---

Heights are how people and programs talk about where something is in the record. A height is short, ordered and human-readable, where a block hash is thirty-two bytes and says nothing about position, so explorers accept a height as a search term and rules are written in terms of heights: the subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks, the difficulty is retargeted every 2,016 blocks, and a coinbase output matures after a hundred. The chapter's own picture of hundreds of thousands of blocks below the one containing Alice's transaction is a statement about height (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A height is not a unique identifier. The book is emphatic: although a single block always has a specific and invariant height, the reverse is not true, because two or more blocks might have the same height while competing for the same position in the chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Only the block hash always names exactly one block. A height is therefore the right way to speak about the record and the wrong way to refer to a particular block when forks matter, which is the subject of the next concept.

slides.title: Fork and alternative block and Double spend

items.head: Fork and alternative block
items.body: A fork, in the sense used here, is the temporary situation in which two or more valid blocks claim the same height, so that the chain briefly has two tips.

rows: ('fork' if a == b else 'extends', max(a, b) + 1)

items.head: Double spend
items.body: A double spend is the attempt to spend the same money twice.

The check itself is a membership test, which the small example performs: if the outpoint named by a new transaction's input is already in the set of spent outputs, the transaction is rejected. Doing this reliably is what the whole branch is for.

slides.notes:
The concept matters for two reasons, one benign and one not. The benign one is that forks happen by themselves, because the network takes time to carry a block to everybody, and a reader who does not expect them will be puzzled when a block briefly disappears from an explorer. The book says that forks are almost always resolved within one block, and that the ten-minute interval is a design compromise between fast confirmation times and the probability of a fork (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The other reason is that a deliberate fork is exactly what a reversal needs, which is the argument the chapter makes about Alice and Bob.

The word fork is badly overloaded and the book warns about it repeatedly. The accidental fork of this concept is not the same as a soft fork or a hard fork, which are changes to the consensus rules, and neither is the same as a software fork of a source repository (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nor is a stale block the same as an orphan block, which the glossary defines as a block whose parent has not yet been processed by the local node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And an accidental fork is not an attack: it is the ordinary consequence of a network with delays.

---

This is the problem Bitcoin was invented to solve, and the chapter's opening sentences are about it: the system does not require trust in third parties, and software on a user's own computer can verify every aspect of its operation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nakamoto's paper puts it at the centre, proposing a solution to the double-spending problem using a peer-to-peer network that timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of proof of work (Nakamoto, 2008). Digital data can be copied, so a purely digital coin can be offered to two people at once; only an agreed order of events can decide which offer counts.

A double spend of a confirmed transaction is not impossible, only expensive, and the book notes that it can only be done on the attacker's own transactions, for which the attacker can produce a valid signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Replacement of an unconfirmed transaction is a different and much cheaper matter: the book's chapter on fees explains that an unconfirmed transaction can be replaced by one paying a higher fee rate, and warns the receiver of an unconfirmed transaction accordingly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And a double spend is not the same as a fork: a fork is two blocks, a double spend is two conflicting transactions.

slides.title: Genesis block

items.head: What it is
items.body: The genesis block is the first block of the blockchain, the one with no parent. The chapter introduces it at the bottom of the stack, saying that below the block containing Alice's transaction are hundreds of thousands of blocks linked to each other in a chain all the way back to block number zero, known as the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: How it works
items.body: Every claim about the block can be recomputed from its fields.

slides.notes:
The genesis block is what makes the chain's security well founded rather than circular. Every other block is trusted because of the work piled on top of it, but the first block has nothing below it, so it is fixed in the software instead. The book explains the consequence: every node always starts with a blockchain of at least one block because the genesis block is statically encoded within Bitcoin Core so that it cannot be altered, every node always knows its hash and structure, the fixed time it was created and even the single transaction within, and thus every node has a secure root from which to build a trusted blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The genesis block is special in ways that break general rules, so it should not be used as an example of an ordinary block. Its previous-block field is all zeros because it has no parent; its reward was never spendable in the usual way; and its presence in the software means that a node does not verify it in the way it verifies every later block, which the book describes by saying that full nodes validate every block after the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Note also that the test networks have genesis blocks of their own, which is why the book shows a different first hash for each of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Unconfirmed transaction
slides.sub: a payment seen by everyone and recorded by nobody

items.head: What it is
items.body: An unconfirmed transaction is one that has been verified and propagated but is in no block.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The arithmetic behind that figure is a multiplication: six blocks at an average of ten minutes each is sixty minutes, as the expression above gives. The important word is average.

slides.notes:
This state is where most of the practical confusion about Bitcoin lives, because it looks like a completed payment and is not yet one. A merchant sees the money arrive in a few seconds and must decide whether to act. The chapter is careful about the two different intervals: within a few seconds Bob sees the transaction on the register, and approximately five minutes after the transaction was first transmitted a miner finds a solution for the block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Those two sentences describe propagation and confirmation, and treating them as the same thing is the error this concept exists to prevent.

Three cautions. An unconfirmed transaction can be replaced, not only ignored: the book's chapter on fees describes replacement by a version paying a higher fee rate and advises the receiver of an unconfirmed transaction accordingly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It can also simply never be mined, if its fee rate is too low for the current market, in which case it may eventually be dropped from the memory pools that hold it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the number of nodes that have seen it is not a measure of safety, because propagation is not confirmation.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Accepting a small payment unconfirmed

items.head: What it is
items.body: Accepting a small payment unconfirmed is the practice of treating a transaction as paid as soon as it has propagated, without waiting for a block. It is not a rule of Bitcoin but a judgement about risk.

rows: 'accept now' if value < threshold else 'wait for confirmations'

items.body: The decision is a comparison, which the small example renders: a value below the threshold is accepted at once, a value at or above it waits.

slides.notes:
The practice matters because it shows that the number of confirmations to require is an economic question, not a technical one. The book offers the comparison that makes it intuitive: it is similar to the practice of coffee shops that accept credit card payments without a signature for amounts below twenty-five dollars, because the risk of a chargeback is low while the cost of delaying the transaction to obtain a signature is comparatively larger (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same chapter draws the opposite conclusion for expensive goods, warning that selling a more expensive item runs the risk of a double-spend attack in which the buyer broadcasts a competing transaction that spends one of the same inputs and cancels the payment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Do not read this practice as a claim that unconfirmed payments are safe. They can be replaced by a version paying a higher fee, as the book's chapter on fees explains, and they can be deliberately double spent by a buyer who is willing to try (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Note also what is being accepted: a payment whose validity has been checked, so the risk is reversal and not forgery. And the threshold is nobody's recommendation; the twenty-five dollars in the comparison is about credit cards, not about Bitcoin, and each merchant must set its own.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Spending the transaction

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: This last group of the branch follows what happens after Alice's payment has been recorded: Bob spends it. The chapter gives the step a section of its own and begins it by saying that now that Alice's transaction has been embedded in the blockchain as part of a block, it is visible to all Bitcoin applications, and each full node can independently verify the transaction as valid and spendable (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group has two concepts, the onward spending itself and the weaker verification that a lightweight client can perform.

The first concept follows Bob, who can now pay a contractor or a supplier by transferring value from Alice's podcast payment to these new owners, and who in doing so extends the chain of transactions; the chapter's…

slides.notes:
The group closes the circle of the chapter. It began with Alice spending an output that Joe had created and ends with Bob spending the output that Alice created, which shows that there is only one mechanism in Bitcoin and that every participant uses it in turn. The chapter says exactly this in its summary: it saw how transactions build a chain that moves value from owner to owner, and tracked Alice's transaction from the moment it was created in her wallet, through the network, to the miners who recorded it on the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Being spendable is not the same as being spent, and being in the blockchain is not the same as being in a wallet's control: Bob can spend the output only because his wallet holds the key that the output's script demands. Note also the one exception to onward spending that this chapter has met, the coinbase output, which must wait a hundred blocks before it can be spent at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Concepts in this section: Spending onward, Simplified payment verification.

slides.title: Spending onward and Simplified payment verification

items.head: Spending onward
items.body: Spending onward is the use of a received output as the input of a new transaction.
The arithmetic is the same subtraction as before.

items.head: Simplified payment verification
items.body: Simplified payment verification is the method by which a program that does not hold the whole blockchain can still gain assurance about a payment.
The efficiency comes from the shape of the merkle tree.

slides.notes:
This step is what makes the word money appropriate. A payment that could be received but not spent again would be a receipt, not a currency; because every received output can become an input, value circulates and the chain of ownership that the chapter opened with continues indefinitely. It is also the step that makes the whole history auditable, since each spending leaves a link that anyone can follow backward to the block in which the bitcoins were first created.

Two cautions. Spending onward needs the key, not just the record: the output is public, but only the holder of the key that satisfies its script can spend it, which is why losing a key loses the funds. And a changeless transaction like Bob's is only practical when the amount to be paid is roughly the amount available minus the fee, as the book says; otherwise the surplus would be handed to the miner (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

---

The method is what makes a Bitcoin wallet possible on a telephone, and it is the clearest example in the course of a deliberate trade between cost and trust. What the client gives up is stated plainly by the book: lightweight clients cannot construct a full picture of all the unspent outputs available for spending because they do not know about all the transactions on the network, and they rely instead on peers to provide partial views of relevant parts of the blockchain on demand (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). What they keep is the ability to tell that work was done committing to their payment, which is the guarantee that this whole branch is about.

The limits of the method must be stated as clearly as its benefit. It proves inclusion and work, not validity: a lightweight client has not checked that the transaction's inputs existed and were unspent, so it is trusting the miners and its peers for that. It also leaks information, since asking peers about particular transactions reveals an interest in them, and the book devotes a section to lightweight clients and privacy for that reason (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The honest summary is the chapter's own word, partially: the client verifies part of what a full node verifies, and knowing which part is the point.

slides.title: Semantics
slides.sub: This branch reads the chapter with the eyes of the course rather than of the book.
slides.notes:
The branch matters for two reasons. The first is academic honesty about what the course is doing: every chapter of this material is turned into an ontology, and a student is entitled to see why the subject suits that treatment. The second is practical. Once a transaction chain is described in a standard vocabulary, questions about it can be asked in a standard query language and answered by a general tool, instead of by a program written for Bitcoin; and the same description can be joined to descriptions of other things, which is what makes a vocabulary worth standardizing.

Two things this branch does not claim. It does not claim that the Bitcoin software uses any of these standards; it does not, and the description here is a model of the chapter's content, built for teaching and for querying. And it does not claim that provenance in this sense identifies anybody: the agents of the model are key holders, and a key holder is not a person until some evidence outside Bitcoin connects them, which is the same caution the first branch gave about addresses.

slides.title: Provenance model

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: A provenance model is a description of where things came from: which things existed, which processes made or changed them, and who was responsible. This group introduces the vocabulary in which such a description is written and then applies it to the chapter.
The group begins with the ontology in general, since a reader must know what kind of thing is being built before seeing one.

slides.notes:
The group is the bridge between this chapter and the method of the course. Bitcoin's blockchain is unusual among records in that its provenance is complete and public: for any output one can follow the chain back to the block in which the bitcoins were created, which is exactly what the chapter says a full node does when it validates every transfer of the funds from the moment the bitcoins were first generated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A record with that property is the ideal case study for a vocabulary designed to express where things came from.

Keep the model and the thing modelled apart. The triples described here are written by this course, not by Bitcoin, and a different modeller could reasonably choose differently: an output might be modelled as an entity or as a state of an entity, and a transaction as one activity or as several. A model is a tool for answering particular questions, so it is judged by whether it answers them, not by whether it is the only possible description.

Concepts in this section: Ontology, Triple and graph, Provenance graph.

slides.title: Ontology
slides.sub: the concept list of this chapter

items.head: What it is
items.body: An ontology, in computing, is an explicit description of the concepts of some area of knowledge and of the relations among them, written in a form that a machine can process.

rows: (len(classes), sum(1 for c in classes if parents.get(c) is None))

items.head: How it works
items.body: The smallest useful description is a list of classes with their parents, which is what the example computes: four classes of which two have no parent, and therefore two roots and a hierarchy below them.

slides.notes:
For this course the ontology is the form in which each chapter is recorded, so that the material can be queried, checked and reused rather than only read. Three benefits follow. Terms are defined once and used consistently, which is why this chapter insists that every technical word it uses is itself a concept. Questions can be stated in advance as competency questions and the description tested against them. And because the vocabulary is standard, the result can be joined to other descriptions, as this branch does by borrowing the provenance vocabulary of the Web consortium.

An ontology is not a database and not a program. It says what kinds of things there are and how they relate, not how to store them efficiently or what to do with them, and a statement in an ontology is a claim about the world that may be wrong. Nor is one ontology ever the ontology of a subject: the same chapter could be modelled with different classes, and this one is organized around how a learner meets the material, which is a pedagogical choice and not a discovery.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Triple and graph

items.head: What it is
items.body: A triple is the unit in which these descriptions are written: a subject, a predicate and an object, read as a single sentence.

rows: (len(triples), len({s for s, p, o in triples} | {o for s, p, o in triples}))

items.head: How it works
items.body: Counting a small graph shows how a description grows.

slides.notes:
Triples are chosen because they combine without planning. Two descriptions written by different people, about different things, can simply be put together, and anything they have in common joins up; nothing has to be merged, because there are no tables and no columns. This is why the provenance standard can be reused here: its predicates for derivation, generation and attribution can be applied to this chapter's outputs and transactions without changing anything in the standard.

Triples are a notation, not a guarantee of truth: a graph records what somebody asserted, so the question of who asserted it, which is itself a provenance question, is always worth asking. A graph is also not a hierarchy, although hierarchies can be expressed in it, and the absence of a triple means only that nothing was said, not that the opposite is true. Finally, the graph of this chapter is a description of the record and not the record: the blockchain itself is a sequence of bytes, and these triples are what this course says about it.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Provenance graph
slides.sub: the chain from Joe to Gopesh as a graph

items.head: What it is
items.body: A provenance graph of this chapter is the transaction chain written in the vocabulary of the provenance standard. The standard's three starting-point classes fit the chapter's parts closely.

rows: [(b, 'wasDerivedFrom', a) for a, b in zip(chain, chain[1:])]

items.body: The translation is mechanical, which is what the executed example shows: a chain of outputs becomes a list of derivation triples, each saying that one output was derived from the one before, so the chain Tx1:0, Tx2:1, Tx3:0 yields two statements.

slides.notes:
Reading the chain this way makes the course's theme visible in the chapter's own material. The chapter says that each input spends an earlier output, that anyone can follow a payment back through the chain of ownership, and that a full node validates every transfer from the moment the bitcoins were first generated in a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Those are statements about derivation, and the provenance vocabulary exists to express exactly them, so Bitcoin's ledger becomes an example of a complete and public provenance record rather than a special case needing its own language.

The model has limits worth stating. Attribution is to a key holder, not to a named person, so the graph does not identify anybody; the chapter's own remark that the change address is often new, for privacy reasons, shows that even the grouping of outputs by owner is a guess (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The activity has a time only once the transaction is in a block, and even then the timestamp is approximate. And derivation here is between whole outputs, not between amounts: an output derived from two inputs does not tell you which satoshi came from where, because the protocol does not record that.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Practice
slides.sub: The last branch of this chapter is about trying things out.
slides.notes:
The branch matters because the central claim of the chapter, that a chain of hashes makes a record expensive to change, is far more convincing when a student breaks a chain with their own hands and watches every block after the change turn invalid. The pages also make the asymmetry of proof of work physical: mining a single demonstration block takes a perceptible moment, and verifying it is instant. For a course this is the cheapest possible laboratory, since the pages run in a browser and risk nothing.

A demonstration is not the system. The pages use a single hash, a difficulty of four leading zeros and a handful of blocks, where Bitcoin uses a double hash, a difficulty astronomically higher and hundreds of thousands of blocks; they have no network, no signatures, no scripts and no fees. Their value is that every simplification is a point of comparison: a student who can say what the page leaves out has understood the chapter.

slides.title: Interactive demonstration

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: An interactive demonstration, in the sense of this group, is a web page that implements a small part of the chapter's mechanics and lets a reader change the inputs and watch the outputs. The group describes the five pages of the Blockchain Demo, whose navigation names them Hash, Block, Blockchain, Distributed and Coinbase, in that order, each page building on the one before (Brownworth, n.d.). The owner's course notes for this chapter give the address of the first of them as the application with which to experience the subject (Altunel, 2021).
The pages work the same way throughout. Each block is a box with fields, the contents of the box are hashed as you type, and the box turns from red to green when its hash satisfies the difficulty.

slides.notes:
The group is included because the chapter's claims are of exactly the kind that a demonstration can settle. That a hash changes completely when one character of the input changes, that a block is valid only when its hash matches a template, that changing an old block invalidates every later one, and that different peers can hold different chains are all statements that can be seen rather than believed. The pages are also a shared reference: a class can be asked to do the same thing and compare results.

Treat the pages as illustrations of single ideas, not as a model of Bitcoin. Their hash is a single SHA-256 rather than the double hash Bitcoin uses, their blocks have no merkle root and no timestamp, their mining is a button rather than a competition, and the amounts in the coinbase page are written as plain numbers with no keys or signatures behind them. The group names these differences for each page so that a learner can translate in both directions.

Concepts in this section: Hash page, Block page, Blockchain page, Distributed page, Coinbase page.

slides.title: Hash page
slides.sub: a digest that changes as you type

items.head: What it is
items.body: The hash page is the first and simplest page of the demonstration. Its content is two fields, labelled Data and Hash, under the heading SHA256 Hash, and the page recomputes the digest of whatever is in the data field as the reader types (Brownworth, n.d.).

The page computes, for a text, the same value that the standard library computes: the digest of the sentence Alice pays Bob 75000 begins 320a22eeeb9c0391, which is the executed example of this concept and can be compared with what the page shows for the same input.

slides.notes:
The page is the right place to start because every later concept of the chapter rests on this one function. The two properties that the chapter attributes to it are both visible within a few keystrokes: that the same input always produces the same output, which the reader sees by typing a text, clearing it and typing it again, and that nobody can predict the output for a new input, which the reader sees by changing a single character and watching the whole digest change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The fixed length is equally visible, since the digest stays sixty-four characters long however much is typed.

Three differences from Bitcoin should be noted while using the page. It applies SHA-256 once, where Bitcoin's identifiers and proof of work apply it twice. It hashes text as typed, where Bitcoin hashes exact binary structures, so a reader cannot reproduce a real transaction identifier by pasting its hexadecimal form into the data box. And a digest on this page is only a digest: it is not a commitment to anything until something refers to it, which is what the next pages add.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Block page
slides.sub: a nonce searched until four zeros appear

items.head: What it is
items.body: The block page puts the hash of the previous page inside a box that has to satisfy a condition. Its fields are a block number, a nonce, a data field and the hash, with a Mine button beside them (Brownworth, n.d.).

rows: next(n for n in range(500000) if h(('1' + str(n) + 'Alice pays Bob 75000').encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0000'))

items.head: How it works
items.body: The page's rule can be reproduced exactly.

slides.notes:
This page is where proof of work stops being a phrase. The reader has already seen that a digest cannot be steered, so the only way to satisfy the condition is to try, and the page does the trying in front of them.
