The asymmetry that the chapter describes, an enormous amount of computation to get right and only a small amount to verify as correct, is experienced as the difference between the pause after pressing Mine and the instant recolouring of the box when the answer is in (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The differences from real mining are large and instructive. There is one miner and no competition, so no block is ever lost to a faster rival. The difficulty is fixed by the page instead of being retargeted every 2,016 blocks. The threshold is expressed as leading zeros rather than as a number below a target, which is a good approximation but not the real rule. And the nonce here is unbounded, whereas Bitcoin's is four bytes and must be supplemented by changing other fields.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Blockchain page and Distributed page

items.head: Blockchain page
items.body: The blockchain page shows five blocks in a column, each with the fields of the block page and one more, labelled Prev, which holds the hash of the block before it (Brownworth, n.d.).

rows: [i for i in range(len(chain)) if i >= edited]

items.head: Distributed page
items.body: The distributed page repeats the five-block chain of the previous page once for each of three peers, labelled Peer A, Peer B and Peer C (Brownworth, n.d.).

slides.notes:
This page demonstrates the single most important claim of the chapter's third branch. The book states it as a chain of consequences: any change to a parent block requires a child block's hash to change, which requires a change in the pointer of the grandchild, which in turn changes the grandchild, and so on, so that once a block has many generations following it, it cannot be changed without forcing a recalculation of all subsequent blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the page this is not an argument but an observation: edit the data of block two and blocks two to five all turn invalid at once.

Note what the page cannot show. There is only one chain and one editor, so there is no competition and no best-chain rule, and nothing stops the reader from patiently remining all five blocks, which in Bitcoin would mean outpacing the entire network while it keeps extending the honest chain. The page also has no transactions, so the thing being protected is only a text; the coinbase page adds a ledger, and the distributed page adds the other participants.

---

The page adds the dimension that the chapter's second branch is about. A chain that only one person holds proves nothing about agreement, whereas three chains that agree show what consensus looks like in the simplest possible case. Tampering with one peer's block two makes that peer's chain disagree with the other two from block two onward, which is the picture behind the chapter's statement that full nodes choose the chain of valid blocks with the most total proof of work when several alternatives exist (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The page leaves out everything about how peers learn from one another: there are no messages, no propagation, no gossip and no rule for choosing between chains, so a reader must supply those from the second and third branches. Nor is there any notion of cumulative work, so the page cannot show why a longer or heavier chain wins; it can only show that disagreement is visible. Three peers are also a very small network, and the chapter's figure of about ten thousand listening nodes is a different order of magnitude (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Coinbase page
slides.sub: a block reward and transactions in each block

items.head: What it is
items.body: The coinbase page is the last of the demonstration and the one closest to Bitcoin.

rows: coinbase - sum(amount for _, _, amount in txs)

items.head: How it works
items.body: Balances on the page are read by adding and subtracting along the chain, which the small example does for one block: a coinbase of one hundred paid to a first party, who then sends thirty to a second and twenty to a third, leaves that party with fifty.

slides.notes:
The page closes the circle of the chapter by putting payments inside the blocks whose security the earlier pages demonstrated. It shows the two things the mining group explains: that new money enters only through the coinbase line, and that everything else is a transfer from one party to another. It also makes tampering meaningful, because changing an amount in an early block now changes who owns what, and the cascade of invalid hashes is the reason that change cannot pass unnoticed.

That last experiment is the page's most useful limitation. There are no keys and no signatures, so anybody can move anybody's money, and there is no check that a sender has what they send, so a double spend is not rejected; Bitcoin prevents both with the scripts and signatures of the first branch and the verification checklist of the second. The amounts are plain numbers rather than outputs, so there are no unspent outputs, no change and no fees. And the coinbase amount here never halves, where Bitcoin's subsidy is cut in half every 210,000 blocks.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 2, How Bitcoin Works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch answers the question that the first two leave open.
The branch matters for two reasons.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.sub: From the chapter's own question bank

items.q: Why do inputs turn separate transactions into a connected history?
options: Because every input names the earlier output it consumes, so a payment can be followed backward
Because every input carries the date on which the earlier transaction was confirmed
Because inputs are numbered consecutively across the whole blockchain
Because an input repeats the amount of the output it spends, so the chain can be summed

items.q: Why is a transaction fee more like a bid in an auction than a price?
options: Because the good being bought is the limited space in a block, not a service with a fixed price
Because miners publish a price list and users accept or reject it
Because the fee is set by the protocol and rises with the amount being sent
Because the fee is returned to the sender if the transaction is not mined

items.q: Why must the serialized form of a transaction be defined to the last detail?
options: Because the identifier is a hash of those bytes and the signature commits to them
Because wallets display the serialized form to the user before signing
Because the serialized form is what a block explorer indexes by address
Because the fee is computed from the number of fields rather than from the amounts

slides.notes:
Answers. (1) A - The reference also lets anyone see whether the same output is being spent twice.  (2) A - The chapter on fees says it is not a fee in the usual sense but much more like a bid for block space.  (3) A - Two programs that serialized the same transaction differently would compute different identifiers.

Every option here is a statement the chapter can judge: there is no filler option, so a student who guesses has to choose between four claims about Bitcoin and defend one.

slides.title: Check yourself, continued
slides.sub: From the chapter's own question bank

items.q: What is the practical rule when a hash does not match between two tools?
options: Reverse the hexadecimal characters of the string
Recompute the hash with a single pass of SHA-256
Try the other byte order before concluding that the data is wrong
Add the missing leading zeros until the length is 64

items.q: What question should a learner keep in mind while reading this group of concepts?
options: What exactly does this tool guarantee, and what does it leave open
Which of these tools makes a transaction secret from other users
Which of these tools is fastest to compute on a telephone
Which of these tools the protocol allows a user to replace

items.q: What is public-key cryptography used for in Bitcoin?
options: To encrypt each payment so that only the receiver can read it
To generate digital signatures, not to encrypt transactions
To compress the blockchain so that nodes need less disk space
To agree a shared secret between the payer's and the payee's wallets

slides.notes:
Answers. (4) C - Reversal is on whole bytes, and Bitcoin displays hashes in one order and stores them in another.  (5) A - The tools differ sharply in what they promise, and none of them is encryption.  (6) B - The book says plainly that it is not used to make the transactions secret.

Every option here is a statement the chapter can judge: there is no filler option, so a student who guesses has to choose between four claims about Bitcoin and defend one.

slides.title: Check yourself, continued
slides.sub: From the chapter's own question bank

items.q: Why is hexadecimal the usual way to print binary data for human eyes?
options: Because it uses fewer characters than any other notation
Because it can represent negative numbers without a sign
Because decimal cannot express values above 255
Because one digit stands for four bits, so two digits are exactly one byte

items.q: What do the links between transactions make possible for any node?
options: Computing the exchange rate at the time of each payment
Finding the name of the person who created each transaction
Recovering a private key from a chain of earlier signatures
Deciding whether an output being spent exists and has not been spent before

items.q: In what sense is a transaction form not a rule of the protocol?
options: The forms are enforced by miners but not by full nodes
The forms apply only to transactions with a change output
The protocol sees only inputs and outputs; the forms are names for typical shapes
The forms were rules in the first version of Bitcoin and were later removed

slides.notes:
Answers. (7) D - Hexadecimal lines up with byte boundaries, which decimal does not.  (8) D - The links turn individual transactions into a history that anyone can check.  (9) C - A transaction can combine the features, for example consolidating many inputs while paying two recipients.

Every option here is a statement the chapter can judge: there is no filler option, so a student who guesses has to choose between four claims about Bitcoin and defend one.
